title: Weldclass backs Ashton Cattach at the 2026 Bathurst 1000
content:
Weldclass is backing Ashton Cattach at the 2026 Repco Bathurst 1000, held at Mount Panorama from 8 to 11 October. Ashton races the #22 Toyota in the Toyota Gazoo Racing Australia GR Cup, and this weekend the car carries the Weldclass logo on the front and rear.

Who is Ashton Cattach?

Ashton is a welder by trade from Melbourne, and he races the #22 Toyota for Ashton Cattach Racing. He arrives at Bathurst 10th in the championship after three rounds and wants to finish the season strong.

That’s a big part of why we’re behind him. He does the same work as a lot of our customers, and welding and racing have more in common than you’d think. Both reward a steady hand and getting the job right the first time. Ashton takes that approach from the workshop to the track.

Bathurst will test it. Mount Panorama runs 6.2 kilometres up and over the mountain, with a steep climb to Skyline and a fast drop down to Conrod Straight. The walls are close the whole way round and there’s very little room for error, which makes a clean weekend worth a lot.

What is the GR Cup?

The GR Cup is one of Australia’s most competitive junior categories. Every driver races the same Toyota GR86, so results come down to talent and racecraft. The series runs on the support card at major Supercars events, including the Bathurst 1000.

How to watch the GR Cup at Bathurst 2026

  • Every session: live on Fox Sports 506 and Kayo.
  • Sunday’s race: also live on Channel 7.

All times are AEDT.

Practice 2Thursday 8 October12:55pm
QualifyingThursday 8 October5:40pm
Race 1Friday 9 October11:15am

Race 3Sunday 11 October9:00am

Bathurst is the second-last round of the 2026 GR Cup. The season wraps up at the Sandown 500 from 6 to 8 November.

Follow the #22

Keep an eye out for the Weldclass #22 on track all weekend. We’ll post updates on our Weldclass Facebook page, and you can follow Ashton Cattach Racing for news from the team.

Good luck, Ashton.

title: Pulse MIG welding: how it works and why it’s worth using
content:
Pulse MIG welding gives you fast, high quality, low spatter welds that look consistently good, with better thermal control than a conventional MIG welder. It is best known as a great process for aluminium. It is also an excellent process for steel, stainless-steel and bronze wires.

In many cases pulse MIG can achieve results comparable to TIG welding, with superior speed and productivity. Below we explain how the process works, where it pays off, the settings you will find on a pulse machine and what to check before you buy one.

How does pulse MIG welding work?

In technical terms, pulse MIG is a highly controlled spray-transfer MIG process. With the traditional short-circuit MIG process the wire touches the weld pool. When pulse welding, the filler metal is transferred from the wire to the weld pool without the wire contacting the pool.

The current alternates, or pulses, between a high peak current and a low background current at a frequency of up to several hundred times per second. With each pulse, the peak current pinches off a droplet of wire and propels it to the weld joint. The background current keeps the arc at a power level low enough that a short circuit can’t occur.

Why use pulse MIG?

Among other benefits, pulse MIG is best known (and most wanted) for these reasons:

  • Lower heat: minimal distortion and reduced burn-through.
  • Reduced spatter: spatter is significantly reduced, or even eliminated, so clean-up is minimal.
  • Visually appealing welds: added value to the finished product.
  • Higher deposition rates: increased efficiency and faster travel speeds.
  • Tighter weld pool control: ideal for out-of-position welding.
  • Reduced welding fumes: a safer and cleaner work environment.

What metals can you weld with pulse MIG?

Pulse MIG is ideal for metals and applications where heat is difficult to control with the standard MIG process, and wherever high weld quality and appearance matter.

Pulse MIG welding aluminium

Aluminium is a high thermal conductor, which means heat is quickly transferred away from the weld pool, and it has a relatively low melting temperature. Pulse MIG gives the operator much greater thermal control to apply enough heat for a successful weld while avoiding distortion or burn-through. Pair it with a quality wire such as PROMAX 5356 aluminium MIG wire.

Pulse MIG welding with bronze wires (MIG brazing)

Bronze wires are typically applied at a temperature lower than the melting point of the parent material. The materials are essentially “stuck” rather than welded together. They are commonly used on thin materials (for example car body panels) where low temperature welding is essential to avoid distortion.

Bronze wires are also commonly used on galvanised or zinc-coated steels up to 2mm thick, because the weld metal does not rust and the lower application temperature prevents disturbance (evaporation) of the zinc coating. The ability to control and reduce heat makes pulse an ideal process for brazing wires.

Pulse MIG welding stainless-steel

Stainless-steel is a poor thermal conductor, so heat is typically trapped close to the weld zone. This can result in expansion and distortion, and rust contamination due to concentrated carbon in the weld zone. The weld pool is comparatively sluggish, with poor wetting and flow into the parent metal.

The pulse process lets stainless wires be applied at lower temperatures to minimise distortion and imperfections. It is especially useful on thin stainless, where avoiding warpage and distortion with the conventional MIG process is often extremely difficult, if not impossible.

Pulse MIG welding mild steel

Mild steel does not present the same thermal challenges as aluminium or stainless, so pulse does not necessarily offer the same advantages here. For this reason, conventional MIG may be the most practical process for mild steel in many applications.

That said, pulse will still reduce spatter and improve weld appearance in many applications. It also gives better control on thin materials and higher deposition rates for faster, more efficient welding, especially on heavier materials.

What is double pulse MIG?

Double pulse is also known as dual pulse or pulse-on-pulse (PoP). It adds an additional pulse wave, where the current alternates (or cycles) between the main current level and a secondary current level. This effectively multiplies the benefits of single pulse, with even better thermal control, weld quality and appearance.

How does pulse MIG compare with TIG welding?

TIG is traditionally the go-to process when materials need to be welded to a higher standard of quality or appearance than conventional MIG delivers. Aluminium and stainless-steel are commonly TIG welded, as these materials are often used where the finish of the final product is critical: boats and marine work, architectural fixtures, food handling equipment and so on.

The disadvantage of TIG is that it is a comparatively slow and inefficient process, which increases cost and processing time. Compared with TIG, pulse MIG offers:

  • Weld quality and finish comparable or very close to TIG in many applications.
  • Superior speed and efficiency.
  • Typically less skill required and easier to learn, which reduces training time.

TIG will always have its place. Even so, pulse MIG is replacing TIG as the logical choice for many applications, especially production work.

Pulse MIG weld cycle, settings and adjustments

If you’re new to pulse MIG, one of your first questions will be what the different parameters and adjustments actually do. The easiest way to answer that is to look at a typical pulse MIG wave, or weld cycle.

Most reputable pulse MIG machines have synergic control, where volts and amps/wire speed are adjusted together automatically. For simplicity, we refer to these collectively as “current” in the table below.

SettingWhat it does
Start currentCurrent level at the start of the weld, usually set as a % of the main current. When welding aluminium it is typically set higher than the main current, to help break through the oxide layer for a clean start.
Start current timeDuration of the start current.
Main currentMain welding current (amps).
Secondary currentAlso known as background current. Applies to double pulse only. Usually set as a % of the main current, and typically lower than the main current for a cooler weld pool.
End currentCurrent level at the end of the weld, usually set as a % of the main current and typically lower than it. End current and end slope work together to prevent or minimise craters for a clean, neat finish (also known as crater fill).
End current timeDuration of the end current.
Start slope timeDuration of the gradual change in output from start current to main welding current.
End slope timeDuration of the gradual change in output from main welding current to end current.
Pulse frequencyDouble pulse only. Adjusts the frequency of the pulse cycle (main current pulse followed by secondary current pulse) in Hz, or cycles per second.
Pulse balanceDouble pulse only. Adjusts the length (%) of the main current pulse within each cycle. Increasing the % makes the main pulse longer and the secondary pulse shorter. As the main current is typically set higher than the secondary current, increasing balance % will usually increase heat.
Arc length (arc control or trim)Adjusts the distance from the end of the wire to the weld pool. If arc length is too short (longer wire stick-out) the arc will be very crackly and produce a lot of spatter. If it is too long, the weld can turn black and porosity can occur.

What should you look for in a pulse MIG welder?

Pulse MIG can open up new work for your workshop or fabrication business and lift your productivity. Pulse is also much more complex and costly than conventional MIG, so it pays to choose a machine that will give you the best results and return on investment over the long term. Keep these points in mind.

Single pulse or double pulse?

Double pulse takes the benefits of single pulse (weld quality, finish and so on) to a new level, and not every pulse MIG has a double pulse mode. Single pulse can be treated as an entry level option if you are learning or trialling pulse MIG. It will typically have fewer features and adjustments and be simpler to operate. More experienced operators may prefer double pulse. Check the machine specs so you know what you’re getting.

Track record

When it comes to developing a truly functional and reliable pulse MIG, many welder manufacturers have tried and failed. Nothing beats experience here. Our advice is to choose a proven machine from a well established manufacturer.

Simple vs complex design

Pulse welding can be less forgiving than conventional MIG. Often it’s the little things, such as a slightly loose connection or an incorrect setting, that decide between a good result and a frustrating waste of time.

It’s easy to be wowed by a long feature list, but every extra feature adds to the list of things that can go wrong. The most reliable and user-friendly pulse machines are typically those with a comparatively simple design.

Controls

It’s common to find operators who were drawn in by the benefits of pulse, then found their machine difficult, confusing and slow to learn. Intuitive controls that are easy to follow maximise your welding time, minimise down time and make it much easier to train new operators.

Wire feed system

With pulse, wire feeding must be 100% consistent and reliable. Reputable drive systems are often made by specialist manufacturers who supply the componentry to welding machine makers, so dig into where a machine’s drive system comes from and its track record.

Solid build matters. Less obvious details are just as critical, such as whether the system is purely mechanical or electronically synchronises with the other machine controls.

Push-pull ready?

For industrial and manufacturing work, a push-pull torch (typically 8m long) is a great way to extend the reach and portability of your machine. This matters most on aluminium, where conventional torches longer than 3m can be troublesome.

With a push-pull torch, the torch pull motor and the machine push motor must be synchronised, so the torch and machine must be compatible. You want a machine that is push-pull ready, and you also want to make sure that:

  1. there’s a push-pull torch available specifically to suit the machine you’re looking at, and
  2. the torch is a tried and tested quality design from an experienced manufacturer, so you get reliability and value from your investment.

  • Pulse mode in all processes: MIG, Stick and TIG.
  • Simple, easy-to-use controls.
  • Strong value, with prices starting from $749 for packages that include a bonus helmet and gloves.

Already own a FURY? Our FURY MPST setup videos walk through the control panel and setting up for aluminium, stainless and gas-shielded MIG. If you need dual pulse for production work, also look at the ULTRA 220MP Dual Pulse MIG welder.

title: Welding fume extractor guide: choosing the right system
content:
Choosing the right welding fume extractor comes down to how and where you weld. Welding fumes are much more than a bit of smoke. They contain fine metal particles, gases and chemical vapours that can seriously affect your health over time.

Australian legislation, enacted in all states of Australia since 2024, is also very tough on fume control. If you weld regularly, you need a plan to manage fumes properly. This guide compares the common methods of controlling welding fume and protecting personnel, by application and by pros and cons, so you can pick the right mix for your workshop.

Fume control solutions overview (video)

In this video we run through the main methods of welding fume extraction and where each is best applied.

Which welding fume extractor suits your application?

The table below compares the common fume extraction and protection methods against their suitability for different applications. “Depends” means it comes down to the capability of the specific unit or model and your specific application.

ApplicationPAPR helmetMobile extractor (LEV)On-torch extractionPortable extractorDowndraft tableWall-mount extractionDucted extraction
Fumes extracted at or close to the sourceNoYesYesYesYesYesYes
Reduces fumes for all workers in the environmentNoYesYesYesYesYesYes
Stationary or localised workYesYesYesDependsYesYesYes
Mobile work or changing locationsYesYesYesYesNoNoNo
MIG: downhand or horizontal positionYesYesYesYesYesYesYes
MIG: vertical and overhead positionYesYesNoYesDependsDependsDepends
TIGYesYesDependsYesYesYesYes
Stick / MMAYesYesNoYesYesYesYes
Plasma and oxy cutting, grinding, gougingYesDependsNoDependsDependsDependsDepends
High fume volume (e.g. some flux-cored wires, frequent use, welding over long periods)YesDependsDependsNoDependsDependsDepends

Fume extractor types compared: advantages and limitations

Here are the key pros and cons of each of the main types of welding fume extraction and protection systems. Browse the full ALLCLEAR fume control range to see the options in each category.

Fume control systemProsCons
Welding helmet with PAPR respirator
  • Relatively low initial purchase cost
  • Very mobile, allows unrestricted movement
  • Quick and easy to deploy
  • Powered air adds operator comfort
  • Only protects the user
  • Does not remove fumes from the environment or protect others in it
  • Depends on battery power
  • Frequent filter replacement and cost
  • Operator carries additional weight and bulk
Mobile fume extractor (LEV)
  • Extracts fumes at the source
  • Can be moved to different locations
  • Versatile: easily deployed and used only where and when each operator needs it
  • Easy to maintain
  • Does not interfere with operator ergonomics or comfort
  • Depending on model and brand, suits a wide range of applications including MIG, Stick, TIG, grinding, plasma, oxy and gouging
  • Must be manually moved to the fume source or welding location
  • In very confined spaces, wall-mounted or other systems may be a better option
  • May not be ideal where the welder moves very frequently over a wide area
Fume extraction MIG or TIG welding torch
  • Extracts fumes directly at the point of generation for high efficiency removal
  • No extra set-up or repositioning, as the extraction point is always at the fume source
  • Not suitable for grinding, Stick/MMA welding, plasma cutting or gouging
  • Typically not suitable for vertical or overhead welding, or where space at the weld joint is confined
  • Torch is bulkier, heavier and more cumbersome than a standard torch (some are better than others)
  • Ongoing cost of torch consumables can be significantly higher than standard torches
Portable extractor
  • Captures fumes directly at the arc or torch
  • High mobility, compact and lightweight
  • Ideal for maintenance, on-site repairs and fieldwork
  • Suits MIG, TIG, Stick and even light cutting, depending on make and model
  • Less suction power and capacity than other systems, so not suitable for high-fume processes or long-duration welding
  • Extraction nozzle or hood must be manually positioned close to the arc
  • Small filter fills quickly and needs frequent cleaning or replacement
Downdraft table
  • Extracts fumes at the source
  • Depending on model and brand, suits a wide range of applications including MIG, Stick, TIG, grinding, plasma, oxy and gouging
  • Hands-free operation that does not interfere with operator ergonomics
  • Ideal for training and production
  • Doubles as a sturdy workbench, saving space and improving workflow
  • Not suitable for large components or structures that can’t be placed on the table
  • Larger tables typically require a 3-phase power supply
  • May not work well for workpieces that block the airflow path or sit too far from the table surface
Ducted or central fume extraction system
  • Extracts fumes at the source
  • Suits large-scale workshops, especially where all workstations are typically active at the same time
  • Minimal maintenance or operator down time
  • High installation cost
  • Time consuming to procure and install
  • Can be inefficient if workstations are used at different times or some are not always used
  • Not suitable where portability and flexibility are required

Helmet, mobile, torch or table: what is the right fume solution for your workshop?

All of these are popular methods of fume control, used in workshops across Australia. Each has strengths and limitations. Here’s a quick summary.

PAPR: personal protection wherever you go

PAPR systems such as the PROMAX 850R welding helmet with PAPR respirator deliver filtered air to the welder through a powered unit and helmet. They are great for almost any welding application and process, whether that is production, mobile work or tight spaces. The cooling effect of powered air also adds comfort in Australia’s hotter climate.

The catch is that PAPR only protects the user. A large percentage of fumes still enters the air, putting others at risk if no other controls are in place.

LEV (mobile extractors): clean air for the whole workshop

Mobile welding fume extractors, like the Weldclass ALLCLEAR range, use extraction arms to pull fumes away from the weld zone. They are highly effective at cleaning the general air and reducing exposure for everyone.

The downside is that LEV relies on precise positioning. If the arm is too far away or knocked out of place, performance drops. It is best suited to localised jobs, and less suited to long weld runs beyond the reach of the hood.

On-torch MIG gun extraction: capture it at the arc

On-torch fume extraction systems capture fumes directly at the arc or torch nozzle. They are ideal for production and repetitive welding.

The drawbacks: they can add weight and bulk to the torch, and they are less effective for vertical welding than for horizontal or downhand work.

Downdraft tables

Downdraft fume extraction tables are ideal for production and education, where a lot of welding happens at a workstation. They intrude very little into the welder’s space. In fact a downdraft table can improve ergonomics beyond fume management by providing a convenient work surface.

On the flip side, downdraft tables are not suitable for workpieces too large to fit on the table surface. For fixed bays, wall-mount extractors are another option to consider.

Stronger together

No single fume solution is perfect for every application. Combined, they give strong, layered protection.

Equipping welders with PAPR helmets, along with a suitable fume extraction system (mobile, torch-mounted or table-based), is standard best practice. It protects workers and helps you comply with legislation that sets strict limits on welding fume exposure.

Get the right fume control set-up

Not sure which combination fits your workshop? Our team can help with quotes, demos and fume control advice. If you want to see how mobile units perform in practice, read do mobile welding fume extractors work?

takeaways: Welding fume contains fine metal particles, gases and chemical vapours, and Australian legislation in all states since 2024 is very tough on fume control.
A PAPR helmet protects only the wearer, while extraction systems remove fumes at or near the source for everyone in the area.

faq.q: Is a PAPR welding helmet enough for fume control?
faq.a: On its own, usually not. A PAPR helmet delivers filtered air to the wearer and suits almost any process, but it only protects the user. A large percentage of fumes still enters the air and puts others at risk. Pair PAPR helmets with a mobile, torch-mounted or table-based extraction system for layered protection.

faq.q: Can on-torch fume extraction be used for all welding?
faq.a: No. On-torch extraction is not suitable for grinding, Stick/MMA welding, plasma cutting or gouging. It is typically not suitable for vertical or overhead welding, or where space at the joint is confined. It works best for production and repetitive MIG welding in the downhand or horizontal position, capturing fume right at the nozzle.

faq.q: When is a downdraft table the right choice?
faq.a: Downdraft tables suit production and education, where a lot of welding happens at a workstation. They extract at the source, run hands-free and double as a sturdy workbench. They are not suited to large components that won't fit on the table, and larger tables typically need a 3-phase power supply.

faq.q: What are the limits of a portable fume extractor?
faq.a: Portable extractors are compact, lightweight and ideal for maintenance, on-site repairs and fieldwork. They have less suction power and capacity than other systems, so they are not suitable for high-fume processes or long-duration welding. The nozzle must be positioned close to the arc, and the small filter needs frequent cleaning or replacement.

faq.q: Is a ducted central extraction system worth it?
faq.a: Ducted systems suit large workshops where all workstations are typically active at the same time, and they need minimal maintenance. They carry a high installation cost, take time to procure and install, and can be inefficient if workstations are used at different times. They are not suitable where you need portability and flexibility.

title: Downdraft table maintenance: schedule and filter care
content:
Good downdraft table maintenance comes down to a few simple habits: check the filter daily, clean it weekly, empty the dust tray before it fills and replace the filter at least once a year. Below is the full schedule we recommend for ALLCLEAR® downdraft fume extraction tables, plus step-by-step procedures for inspecting, cleaning and replacing filters safely.

The schedule is written for the Weldclass models listed below. Many of the steps are general best practice, so they will also apply to other brands of downdraft tables and welding fume extractor tables.

Which downdraft tables does this schedule cover?

This information applies to the following Weldclass ALLCLEAR models:

  • ALLCLEAR® TA100 fume extraction grinding and welding table (disposable filter)
  • ALLCLEAR® TA400 fume extraction grinding and welding table (auto cleaning)
  • ALLCLEAR® TA500 fume extraction grinding and welding table (auto cleaning)
  • ALLCLEAR® FP Series downdraft fixture point table (cleanable filter)

Downdraft table maintenance schedule

Work through these checks at the intervals shown. Where a task says to follow a process below, use the matching procedure in the next section.

FrequencyAction / componentDetails
DailyVisual inspectionCheck for any visible damage or wear. Ensure all components and surfaces (including the top and underside of the table top) are free from obstruction and debris.
DailyFilter checkInspect the filter. If visibly clogged, clean and/or replace*. Replace if damaged. Follow the processes below.
DailyFunction checkTurn the unit on and check for normal operation and airflow at the table top and exhaust outlet. Test the emergency stop. Auto clean models only: test that the auto clean function is operating by switching the unit off (power must be connected and switched on).
DailyAir supply (auto clean models only)Ensure the compressed air supply is connected and supply pressure is between 3 and 4 bar. Ensure the air hose, air filter and air compressor are operating correctly and in good condition.
DailyCheck dust collection tray levelIf your unit has a dust collection tray or bin, open the tray/bin and empty it if filled to more than 25% of capacity. Follow the process below.
WeeklyClean filter (units with cleanable filter only)Clean the filter* as per the process below.
WeeklyAir supply (auto clean models only)Check for and rectify any wear or leaks in hoses and connections. Follow the air compressor and air filter manufacturer’s recommendations for regular checks and maintenance. Replace the air filter cartridge if required.
WeeklyPower supplyCheck the power supply cable and connections for signs of wear or damage. Ensure plugs and connections are secure and tight.
WeeklyClean exteriorThoroughly clean all external components and surfaces with a suitable brush and/or cloth/rag. If the optional external carbon filter is installed, clean it with an air gun.
WeeklyEmpty dust collection trayEmpty the tray/bin, following the process below.
AnnualReplace filterReplace the filter as per the process below, if this has not occurred within the last 12 months.
AnnualAir supply (auto clean models only)Replace the air hose if there are any signs of wear, cracking or perishing. Follow the air compressor and air filter manufacturer’s recommendations for annual servicing and replacement of parts.
AnnualPower supplyFollow WorkSafe and your employer’s guidelines for applicable test and tag of the input cable and plug.
AnnualUpdate recordsEnsure maintenance tasks are, or have been, logged. Review records to ensure compliance with this schedule.

*The TA100 has a disposable filter only. Replace it when full. It is not designed to be cleaned.

How do you inspect, clean and replace a downdraft table filter?

Use these guidelines whenever you inspect, clean or replace a filter. Always read them alongside the instruction manual for your ALLCLEAR downdraft table.

Safety first: before you start

  • Always disconnect the unit from the mains power supply before starting any filter maintenance.
  • Carry out maintenance only in a well-ventilated environment.
  • Make sure the unit and cleaning area are well shielded from wind or strong airflow, so dust is not disturbed.
  • Maintenance should be done by authorised and trained personnel only.
  • Operators must wear respiratory protection conforming to AS/NZS 1716 class P2 or P3, plus hand/body protection and eye protection.
  • Other personnel must stand well away from, and not make contact with, the unit, the filter and the extracted matter.
  • When disposing of dust and/or filters, follow local regulations for disposal of contaminated materials.

Filter inspection

  1. Follow the safety instructions above and all applicable instructions in the instruction manual.
  2. Open the filter cleaning access door/s or tray/s to inspect the filter/s.
  3. Check for signs of filter clogging, damaged filter material, tears, punctures and similar damage.

Filter cleaning: FP Series

  1. Follow the safety instructions above and all applicable instructions in the instruction manual.
  2. Turn the unit off and disconnect it from the power supply.
  3. Open the filter access door.
  4. Prepare a suitable containment bag, such as a heavy-duty disposable non-porous plastic bag.
  5. Remove the filter and place it in the containment bag. Avoid excess movement or agitation of the filter while placing it in the bag.
  6. Keep the filter in the bag during cleaning and hold the mouth of the bag closed to minimise escaping dust and debris. It is generally best to clean the filter outdoors so any escaping dust does not re-enter the workplace.
  7. Using a suitable compressed air gun, direct air evenly from the inside of the cartridge filter towards the outside. Do not push the air gun directly into or against the filter, as this may damage it.
  8. Apply air for 5-10 minutes, covering the whole filter surface as evenly and thoroughly as possible.
  9. Re-install the filter (refer to the instruction manual).
  10. Reconnect the unit to the power supply.

Filter cleaning: auto cleaning models (including TA400 and TA500)

ALLCLEAR auto cleaning units use a pulse cleaning system. It accumulates, then releases, a burst of compressed air inside the filter to push particles out of it.

  • Follow the safety instructions above and all applicable instructions in the instruction manual.
  • The auto clean cycle activates every time the unit is turned off (the power supply must remain connected and switched on), or when the unit detects a reduction in airflow based on pressure differential.
  • To trigger a clean cycle, turn the unit off at the control panel while it remains connected to the power supply. You will hear a mild explosion-like noise from inside the machine as the air pulse is released.
  • If suction or airflow at the intake is visibly reduced or reducing, and/or the malfunction alarm keeps sounding at frequent intervals, the filter needs to be cleaned manually (see the process above) or replaced.

Filter replacement: cleanable filter models (including TA400, TA500 and FP Series)

Replace the filter if any part of it is damaged, if there is a puncture or tear in the filter medium, if it becomes clogged and cleaning is no longer effective, if the full filter indicator still displays after cleaning, or if it has not been replaced in the last 12 months.

  1. Turn the unit off and disconnect it from the power supply.
  2. Follow the safety instructions above and all applicable instructions in the instruction manual.
  3. Before replacing the cartridge filter, prepare a suitable container for disposal, such as a heavy-duty PE bag or plastic bag.
  4. Open the main filter access door.
  5. Unscrew the filter retaining bolt/s and remove the cartridge holder.
  6. Pass the disposal bag over the filter before removing it from the compartment.
  7. Seal the mouth of the bag with a cable tie or similar, then dispose of the old filter.
  8. Install the new filter and make sure it is properly seated.
  9. Close and lock the filter access door.
  10. Reconnect the unit to the power supply.

Filter replacement: disposable filter models (including TA100)

Replace the filter if any part of it is damaged, if there is a puncture or tear in the filter medium, if it becomes clogged and cleaning is no longer effective, if the full filter indicator still displays after cleaning, or if it has not been replaced in the last 12 months.

  1. Follow the safety instructions above and all applicable instructions in the instruction manual.
  2. Turn the unit off and disconnect it from the power supply.
  3. Before replacing the filter, prepare a suitable containment bag (such as a heavy-duty disposable bag) for disposal.
  4. Open the main filter tray/drawer.
  5. Remove the filter and place it in the containment bag.
  6. Seal the mouth of the bag with a cable tie or similar, then dispose of the old filter.
  7. Install the new filter and make sure it is properly seated.
  8. Close the filter tray/drawer.
  9. Reconnect the unit to the power supply.

Emptying the dust collection tray or bin

  1. Follow the safety instructions above and all applicable instructions in the instruction manual.
  2. Turn the unit off and disconnect it from the power supply.
  3. Remove the dust collection tray or bin.
  4. Empty the tray/bin into a heavy-duty non-porous disposable bag (such as a PE bag), seal the bag permanently with a cable tie or similar, then dispose of it.
  5. Re-fit the tray or bin to the machine.
  6. Reconnect the unit to the power supply.

Where do you get replacement filters and spare parts?

Replacement filters for all ALLCLEAR units are listed under filters for ALLCLEAR fume extraction units. Hoses, fittings and other parts are in the ALLCLEAR spare parts range.

Running other ALLCLEAR gear as well? See our maintenance schedule for mobile welding fume extractors, and there is a matching schedule for on-torch extractors. If you are weighing up a new unit, how to check a fume extractor’s suction power is worth a read first.

Keep your table pulling its weight

A downdraft table only protects your team while air is moving through it. Print this schedule, log every task and keep a spare filter on the shelf. For filters, parts or advice on a new table, find your nearest Weldclass distributor or get in touch with our team.

takeaways: Check the filter, airflow, emergency stop and dust tray level every day.
Auto clean models need a compressed air supply of 3 to 4 bar to run their pulse cleaning cycle.
Empty the dust tray once it is more than 25% full, and replace filters at least every 12 months.
The TA100 uses a disposable filter that must be replaced when full and never cleaned.
Wear AS/NZS 1716 class P2 or P3 respiratory protection and disconnect power for all filter work.

faq.q: How often should a downdraft table filter be replaced?
faq.a: Replace the filter at least once every 12 months. Replace it sooner if it is damaged, punctured or torn, if it is clogged and cleaning no longer works, or if the full filter indicator keeps showing after cleaning. On the ALLCLEAR TA100, which has a disposable filter, replace it whenever it is full.

faq.q: What air pressure do ALLCLEAR auto clean downdraft tables need?
faq.a: Auto clean models such as the TA400 and TA500 need a compressed air supply connected at between 3 and 4 bar. Check this daily, along with the condition of the air hose, air filter and compressor, so the pulse cleaning system can clear the filter properly every time the unit is switched off.

faq.q: How do I trigger the auto clean cycle on a TA400 or TA500?
faq.a: Turn the unit off at the control panel while it stays connected to a switched-on power supply. You will hear a mild explosion-like noise as the air pulse fires inside the filter. The cycle also runs automatically when the unit detects reduced airflow based on pressure differential.

faq.q: What PPE do I need to clean a downdraft table filter?
faq.a: Wear respiratory protection conforming to AS/NZS 1716 class P2 or P3, along with hand and body protection and eye protection. Disconnect mains power first, work in a well-ventilated area shielded from wind, and keep other people well away from the unit, the filter and the extracted dust.

faq.q: When should I empty the dust collection tray?
faq.a: Check the tray or bin level every day and empty it if it is more than 25% full. Empty it weekly regardless. Disconnect power, tip the contents into a heavy-duty non-porous bag such as a PE bag, seal it permanently with a cable tie and dispose of it under local regulations.

title: On-torch fume extractor maintenance schedule
content:
On-torch fume extractor maintenance comes down to a few minutes each day and a slightly longer check each week. This is our recommended daily, weekly and annual schedule for Weldclass ALLCLEAR® on-torch and portable fume extractors, with step-by-step procedures for inspecting, cleaning and replacing the filter and emptying the dust tray. It is written for the models listed, but many of the steps are general best practice for other brands too.

Want a printed copy for the workshop? Download this maintenance schedule as a PDF.

Which ALLCLEAR models does this schedule cover?

This schedule applies to the following Weldclass ALLCLEAR® on-torch and portable extractors:

  • ALLCLEAR® MT31
  • ALLCLEAR® MT84

On-torch fume extractor maintenance schedule

FrequencyAction / componentDetails
DailyVisual inspectionCheck for any visible damage or wear. Make sure all components and surfaces are free from obstruction and debris.
DailyFilter check*Inspect the filter. If visibly clogged, clean and/or replace it. Replace if damaged. Follow the procedures below.
DailyFunction checkTurn the unit on and check for normal operation and airflow at the hose or nozzle intake and the exhaust outlet. Test the emergency stop.
DailyCheck dust collection tray levelOpen the dust collection tray or bin and empty it if it is more than 25% full. Follow the procedure below.
DailyTorch checkCheck the torch or gun for any visible signs of damage, wear or airflow obstruction. Replace torch consumables if worn or affected by spatter build-up.
WeeklyPower supplyCheck the power supply cable and connections for signs of wear or damage. Make sure plugs and connections are secure and tight.
WeeklyClean exteriorThoroughly clean all external components and surfaces with a suitable brush and/or cloth.
WeeklyEmpty dust collection trayEmpty the tray or bin following the procedure below.
WeeklyInspect hoses, torch, etcCheck all hoses and fittings (including the torch hose) for signs of damage, cracks, air leaks and the like. Replace parts as required.
AnnualReplace filter*Replace the filter following the procedure below, if this has not been done within the last 12 months.
AnnualPower supplyFollow WorkSafe and your employer’s guidelines for applicable testing and tagging of the input power cable and plug.
AnnualUpdate recordsMake sure maintenance tasks have been logged. Review records to confirm compliance with this schedule.

*Including any prefilters or spark filters, if applicable to your unit.

How do you inspect, clean and replace the filter?

Follow these guidelines when inspecting, cleaning or replacing a filter. Also consult and follow the instruction manual for your ALLCLEAR welding fume extractor.

Safety first: before you start

  • Always disconnect the unit from the mains power supply before starting any filter maintenance.
  • Carry out maintenance only in well-ventilated areas.
  • Make sure the unit and cleaning area are well shielded from wind or strong airflow, so dust is not disturbed.
  • Maintenance should be carried out by authorised and trained personnel only.
  • Operators must wear appropriate respiratory protection conforming to AS/NZS 1716 class P2 or P3, plus hand and body protection and eye protection.
  • Make sure other personnel stand well away from, and do not touch, the unit, the filter and the extracted matter.
  • When disposing of dust and/or filters, follow local regulations for disposal of contaminated materials.

Filter inspection

  1. Follow the safety instructions above and all applicable instructions in the instruction manual.
  2. Open the unit and remove the filter (refer to the instruction manual).
  3. Check the filter for signs of clogging, damaged filter medium or material, tears, punctures and the like.
  4. Clean or replace the filter if required (see the instructions below).
  5. Re-install the filter (refer to the instruction manual).
  6. Reconnect the unit to the power supply.

Filter cleaning

  1. Follow the safety instructions above and all applicable instructions in the instruction manual.
  2. Prepare a suitable containment bag, such as a heavy-duty, disposable, non-porous plastic bag.
  3. Open the unit, remove the filter and place it in the containment bag. Avoid any excess movement or agitation of the filter while placing it in the bag.
  4. Keep the filter in the containment bag during cleaning, and hold the mouth of the bag closed to minimise escaping dust and debris. It is generally best to clean the filter outdoors so any escaping dust does not re-enter the workplace.
  5. Using a suitable compressed air gun, direct the air evenly from the inside of the cartridge filter towards the outside. Do not push the air gun directly into or against the filter, as this may damage it.
  6. Apply the air for 5-10 minutes, covering the whole filter surface as evenly and thoroughly as possible.
  7. Re-install the filter (refer to the instruction manual).
  8. Reconnect the unit to the power supply.

Filter replacement

Replace the filter if:

  • any part of the filter is damaged
  • there is a puncture or tear in the filter medium or material
  • the filter becomes clogged and cleaning is no longer effective
  • the full filter indicator continues to display even after cleaning
  • the filter has not been replaced in the last 12 months.

Replacement filters and other ALLCLEAR spare parts are available through our distributors. To replace the filter:

  1. Follow the safety instructions above and all applicable instructions in the instruction manual.
  2. Before replacing the main cartridge filter, prepare a suitable container for disposal (such as a heavy-duty PE bag or plastic bag).
  3. Open the unit and remove the filter (refer to the instruction manual).
  4. Place the filter in the disposal bag or container. Seal the mouth of the bag with a cable tie or similar.
  5. Install the new filter and make sure it is properly seated (refer to the instruction manual).

Emptying the dust collection tray or bin

  1. Follow the safety instructions above.
  2. Open the unit to access the dust collection tray or bin (see the instruction manual).
  3. Empty the tray or bin into a heavy-duty, non-porous disposable bag (such as a PE bag), seal the bag permanently with a cable tie or similar, then dispose of it.
  4. Re-assemble the unit and connect it to the mains power supply.

Keep the torch end in good shape

On an on-torch extractor, the torch is part of the extraction system. Worn consumables or spatter build-up at the torch can obstruct airflow, so the daily torch check matters as much as the filter check. If airflow is still low after a clean, read does your welding fume extractor really suck, or contact our fume team for help. Running mobile units too? Follow our mobile fume extractor maintenance schedule, and see how mobile fume extractors compare with on-torch extraction.

faq.q: How often should an on-torch fume extractor be serviced?
faq.a: Do a visual inspection, filter check, function check, dust tray check and torch check every day. Each week, check the power supply, clean the exterior, empty the dust tray and inspect all hoses and fittings. Annually, replace the filter if it has not been replaced in 12 months, test and tag the power cable and plug, and review your records.

faq.q: How do I clean the filter on an ALLCLEAR MT31 or MT84?
faq.a: Disconnect power, then remove the filter and place it in a heavy-duty non-porous bag. Keep the bag mouth held closed and, ideally, work outdoors. Direct compressed air evenly from the inside of the cartridge towards the outside for 5-10 minutes, without pushing the air gun into the filter. Re-install the filter and reconnect power.

faq.a: Replace it if any part is damaged, if the filter medium is punctured or torn, if it is clogged and cleaning no longer works, or if the full filter indicator keeps displaying after cleaning. Replace it at least every 12 months regardless. This applies to any prefilters or spark filters fitted to your unit as well.

faq.q: Why does the torch need checking every day?
faq.a: On an on-torch extractor, fume is drawn in at the torch, so damage, wear or an airflow obstruction there affects extraction. The daily check looks for visible damage, wear or blockages on the torch or gun. Replace torch consumables when they are worn or affected by spatter build-up, and inspect the torch hose for cracks or leaks weekly.

faq.q: What PPE is needed for fume extractor filter maintenance?
faq.a: Wear respiratory protection conforming to AS/NZS 1716 class P2 or P3, along with hand and body protection and eye protection. Work only in well-ventilated areas shielded from wind, keep other people well away from the unit and the extracted matter, and dispose of dust and filters according to local regulations for contaminated materials.

title: Fume extractor maintenance schedule for mobile units
content:
Regular fume extractor maintenance keeps a mobile unit pulling full airflow and keeps the people servicing it safe. Below is our recommended daily, weekly and annual schedule for Weldclass ALLCLEAR® mobile welding fume extractors (also known as LEVs, or local exhaust ventilation), followed by step-by-step procedures for inspecting, cleaning and replacing the filter and emptying the dust tray. It is written for the models listed, but many of the steps are general best practice for other brands of mobile welding fume extractor too.

Want a copy for the workshop wall? Download this maintenance schedule as a PDF.

Which ALLCLEAR models does this schedule cover?

This schedule applies to the following Weldclass ALLCLEAR® mobile extractors:

  • ALLCLEAR® MA100
  • ALLCLEAR® MA300 AUTO
  • ALLCLEAR® MA350 STD
  • ALLCLEAR® MA350 AUTO

Mobile fume extractor maintenance schedule

FrequencyAction / componentDetails
DailyVisual inspectionCheck for any visible damage or wear. Make sure all components and surfaces are free from obstruction and debris.
DailyFilter checkInspect the filter. If visibly clogged, clean and/or replace it. Replace if damaged. Follow the procedures below.
DailyFunction checkTurn the unit on and check for normal operation and airflow at the arm/hood intake and the exhaust outlet. Test the emergency stop. On auto clean models only, test that the auto clean function operates by switching the unit off (power must stay connected and switched on).
DailyAir supply (auto clean models only)Make sure the compressed air supply is connected and supply pressure is between 3 and 4 bar. Check the air hose, air filter and air compressor are operating correctly and in good condition.
DailyCheck dust collection tray levelOpen the dust collection tray or bin and empty it if it is more than 25% full. Follow the procedure below.
WeeklyAir supply (auto clean models only)Check for and fix any wear or leaks in hoses and connections. Follow the air compressor and air filter manufacturer’s recommendations for regular checks and maintenance. Replace the air filter cartridge if required.
WeeklyPower supplyCheck the power supply cable and connections for signs of wear or damage. Make sure plugs and connections are secure and tight.
WeeklyClean exteriorThoroughly clean all external components and surfaces with a suitable brush and/or cloth. If the optional external carbon filter is installed, clean it with an air gun.
WeeklyClean filterClean the filter following the procedure below.
WeeklyEmpty dust collection trayEmpty the tray or bin following the procedure below.
WeeklyInspect armCheck the suction arm for signs of damage, cracks, air leaks and the like. Replace parts as required.
AnnualReplace filterReplace the filter following the procedure below, if this has not been done within the last 12 months.
AnnualAir supplyReplace the air hose if it shows any signs of wear, cracking or perishing. Follow the air compressor and air filter manufacturer’s recommendations for annual servicing and replacement of parts.
AnnualPower supplyFollow WorkSafe and your employer’s guidelines for applicable test and tag of the input cable and plug.
AnnualUpdate recordsMake sure maintenance tasks have been logged. Review records to confirm compliance with this schedule.

How do you inspect, clean and replace the filter?

Follow these guidelines when inspecting, cleaning or replacing a filter. Also consult and follow the instruction manual for your ALLCLEAR mobile fume extractor.

Safety first: before you start

  • Always disconnect the unit from the mains power supply before starting any filter maintenance.
  • Carry out maintenance only in well-ventilated areas.
  • Make sure the unit and cleaning area are well shielded from wind or strong airflow, so dust is not disturbed.
  • Maintenance should be carried out by authorised and trained personnel only.
  • Operators must wear appropriate respiratory protection conforming to AS/NZS 1716 class P2 or P3, plus hand and body protection and eye protection.
  • Make sure other personnel stand well away from, and do not touch, the unit, the filter and the extracted matter.
  • When disposing of dust and/or filters, follow local regulations for disposal of contaminated materials.

Filter inspection

  1. Follow the safety instructions above.
  2. Open the rear filter cleaning access door to inspect the internal (outlet) surface of the filter.
  3. Open the main (front) door to inspect the external (inlet) surface of the main filter.
  4. Check for signs of clogging, damaged filter material, tears, punctures and the like.

Filter cleaning: manual cleaning models

  1. Follow the safety instructions above.
  2. Make sure the rear filter cleaning access door is closed.
  3. Open the main (front) door.
  4. Using a suitable compressed air gun, direct the air evenly from the inside of the cartridge filter towards the outside. Do not push the air gun directly into or against the filter, as this may damage it.
  5. Apply the air for 5-10 minutes, covering the whole filter surface as evenly and thoroughly as possible.
  6. Close the main door.
  7. Reconnect the unit to the power supply.

Filter cleaning: auto cleaning models

Follow the safety instructions above. ALLCLEAR auto cleaning units use a pulse cleaning system, which accumulates and then releases a burst of compressed air inside the filter to push particles out of it.

  • The auto clean cycle activates every time the unit is turned off (the power supply must remain connected and switched on), or when the unit detects a reduction in airflow based on pressure differential.
  • To trigger a clean cycle, turn the unit off at the control panel while it stays connected to the power supply. You will hear a mild explosion-like noise from inside the machine as the air pulse is released.
  • If suction at the intake hood is visibly reduced or reducing, and/or the malfunction alarm keeps sounding at frequent intervals, the filter needs to be cleaned manually (see the procedure above) or replaced.

Filter replacement

Replace the filter if it is damaged, or when it becomes clogged and cleaning is no longer effective. Shorter or continuous warning alarm intervals, even after automatic and/or manual cleaning, also indicate this. Genuine ALLCLEAR replacement filters and spare parts are available through our distributors.

  1. Follow the safety instructions above.
  2. Before replacing the cartridge filter, prepare a suitable container for disposal (such as a heavy-duty PE bag or plastic bag).
  3. Open the main filter access door.
  4. Unscrew the retaining bolt of the cartridge holder and remove the cartridge holder.
  5. Pass the disposal bag over the cartridge filter before removing the cartridge from the compartment. Seal the mouth of the bag with a cable tie or similar.
  6. Insert the new cartridge filter. Make sure the cartridge filter and gasket are properly seated.
  7. Insert the cartridge holder and secure the cartridge with the fixing bolt.
  8. Close and lock the filter access door.
  9. Connect the filter unit to the mains power supply.

Emptying the dust collection tray or bin

Follow the safety instructions above. On the MA100, the unit must be turned off and disconnected. On the MA300 and MA350 models, the bin can be emptied while the machine is running.

  1. Remove the dust collection tray or bin.
  2. Empty the tray or bin into a heavy-duty, non-porous disposable bag (such as a PE bag), seal the bag permanently with a cable tie or similar, then dispose of it.
  3. Refit the tray or bin to the machine.

Keep it logged and keep it running

Log every task as you go. Up-to-date records are how you show your fume controls are being maintained to this schedule. If your suction has dropped and cleaning is not bringing it back, read does your welding fume extractor really suck or contact our fume team for advice. Running on-torch units as well? Use our on-torch fume extractor maintenance schedule.

title: Welder plug size: 10A vs 15A on single-phase power
content:
The right welder plug size depends on the machine’s effective input current rating (I1eff), shown on the data plate. Under the Australian standard, a welder rated at 10A I1eff or less can be fitted with a 10A plug, and one rated above 10A and up to 15A should have a 15A plug. Below we cover the questions we hear most often from users of single-phase welding machines and plasma cutters: can I use a 10A plug on my welder, why does my circuit breaker keep tripping, why does my machine cut out, and what size plug or power supply should I use?

This is a complex topic to explain in full. We’ve kept it in plain, layman’s terms. For complete technical detail, refer to the Australian standard mentioned below.

Why do welders trip breakers on 10A single-phase power?

Welders are power-hungry compared with most common power tools, and 10 Amp power can only supply a limited amount of current. That conflict can trip circuit breakers, or make the welder cut out when it reaches its duty cycle limit.

Supply voltage varies more than you think

  • The Australian standard for single-phase power is 230V, but the output at any wall socket can vary from one location to another, or even at different times of the day. Variations from 200V to 250V, or wider, are not uncommon.
  • Changes in supply voltage (V) change the current draw (A) of the welding machine, which also changes its duty cycle. If supply voltage drops, the machine draws more power. If supply voltage rises, it draws less.

Current draw depends on more than the amps setting

The output setting is only one factor in how much current a welder draws. Others include:

  • the power supply (as above)
  • ambient temperature
  • operator technique
  • the type of shielding gas, which influences weld temperature
  • the type and size of wire or electrode used.

How do I stop my welder tripping the breaker or cutting out?

If your welder frequently trips circuit breakers or cuts out because it is exceeding its duty cycle, try these:

  • Reduce the amperage output setting. The higher the amperage, the more power the machine draws.
  • Consider Type-D circuit breakers (often called slow-blow breakers). A D-curve breaker is designed to tolerate 10-20 times its rated current for a short period before tripping. D-curve breakers are recommended to prevent nuisance tripping, particularly for 180A and larger welding machines. Breaker changes are a job for a qualified electrician.

What size plug does my welder need?

The Australian standard AS60974.1 Arc welding equipment: Welding power sources states that the plug and power input cable should be rated to the machine’s effective input current. That figure is usually shown on the data plate with the symbol I1eff.

Effective input current (I1eff) on the data platePlug to fit
10A or less10A plug
More than 10A, up to 15A15A plug
Higher ratingsAnd so on, matched to the I1eff rating

The higher the machine’s output capacity (amps), the higher its I1eff rating will be. Efficiency, power factor, functions and processes, and duty cycle also change the I1eff rating from one model or brand to another.

What is effective input current (I1eff)?

In very simple terms, I1eff is something like an average or median current draw. The formula behind it is complex and depends on duty cycle, efficiency, power factor, maximum output and other parameters.

Don’t confuse I1eff with the maximum or peak current draw (I1max), which is always higher. For example, a machine might have an I1eff rating of 15A and an I1max rating of 32A.

I1eff also takes into account the full, or maximum, output range of the machine. When you weld below maximum output or duty cycle, the actual current draw at that moment is lower than the I1eff rating on the data plate.

Can I fit a 10A plug to a 15A welder?

This is the question we get most. People want to fit a smaller plug, such as a 10A plug on a machine designed for a 15A plug, so they can run it from a more convenient power supply. Here is what you need to know.

Actual current draw follows the output you use

If a 15A-rated machine is only used at relatively low output or duty cycle, the actual effective current draw at that time may be 10A or less. On that basis, some users argue a 10A plug can be used for that application.

Take our FORCE 205MST multi-process welder, a 200A machine with an I1eff rating of 15A based on full output. If you only use it at around 140A output at 15% duty cycle, the actual current draw will be less than 10A.

Machines with dual ratings and power programs

Some larger machines on the market (for example 250A and above) carry two output ratings on the data plate. These show the maximum output to use for different plug and circuit sizes. A 250A machine might have an I1eff rating of around 20-30A at full output, plus additional ratings showing the maximum output that keeps I1eff at 15A for use with a 15A plug.

Some Weldclass machines have special programs that change the machine output to suit different power outlets:

  • ULTRA 210MST MIG welder: 10A and 15A programs
  • ULTRA 202T AC/DC TIG welder: 10A and 15A programs
  • FORCE 290MST MIG welder: 15A and 32A programs

What happens if you overdraw the circuit?

If the machine isn’t used at high output or high duty cycle, its current draw stays down. As long as the actual effective current draw is no higher than the rating of the power circuit you’re using, everything can be expected to operate normally.

Weld at high amps, or at high duty cycle (welding often or for long periods), and current draw rises. Once actual current draw exceeds the rating of the circuit or outlet, the circuit breaker will likely trip.

Overdrawing a power circuit, especially excessively or repeatedly, also risks overheating the supply circuit components and creating a fire hazard. That is why you should know and comply with the AS60974.1 I1eff rating requirements.

Will it damage my welder?

Using a 15A-rated machine on a 10A supply is unlikely to damage the welding machine itself, because it is effectively running below full capacity. The risk sits with the supply. If current draw exceeds the rating of the 10A circuit or outlet, the wiring, socket or plug can overheat and burn out, creating a fire hazard. Insurance may be voided for incidents where an incorrect power supply is deemed to have been used.

Will a 10A plug damage a 15A outlet?

No. The only major difference between a 10A and a 15A plug is the size of the earth pin. The earth pin is a safety feature and does not normally carry any current. The larger pin on a 15A plug is there simply to stop it being plugged into a 10A outlet.

What about generator power?

Generators bring their own set of rules. See our guide to running inverter welders on generators before you weld off one.

Choosing a welder for your power supply

Check the I1eff rating on the data plate before you buy, and match it to the outlets you actually have. If you’re not sure which machine suits your workshop or site power, try our welding machine selector, or talk to the Weldclass team. When you’re ready, find a Weldclass distributor near you.

All applicable safety standards (including Australian standards), industry guidelines and regulations should be consulted and followed. This article is intended to assist readers who do not have technical expertise or training (such as electrical engineering qualifications) with a basic understanding of the topics presented, and as such some terminology may be imprecise, and the information given will not be a complete or exhaustive resource. title: TIG welding tips: 9 rules of thumb from a WorldSkills medallist
content:
The most useful TIG welding tips usually aren’t in the manual. They’re learned on the job, passed down by experienced tradies or discovered the hard way. Here are nine rules of thumb that make TIG welding a lot easier, especially when you’re starting out, covering gas flow, tungsten stick-out, post-flow, amperage, practice and weld colour.

They come from Andrew Barnes. Andrew is Australia’s first Bronze Medal winner, a former Australian National Judge, and former International Chief Judge of the WorldSkills International Welding Competition.

1. How much gas flow do I need for TIG?

Set your shielding gas flow rate to match the internal diameter (ID) of your gas nozzle.

Rule of thumb: 1 LPM of gas per 1mm of nozzle ID.

Example: a 12.7mm nozzle = approx. 13 LPM of gas.

2. How far should the tungsten stick out with a gas lens?

When you’re using a gas lens, your tungsten stick-out should equal the inside diameter of the nozzle.

Example: using a 25mm nozzle? Your tungsten stick-out should also be around 25mm.

3. How long should TIG post-flow be?

Adequate post-flow gas protects your tungsten after the arc stops.

Rule of thumb: if your machine has post-gas time control, set 5 seconds of post-flow for every 1mm of tungsten diameter.

Example: a 2.4mm tungsten = 5 x 2.4 = 12 seconds of post-flow.

4. Practise the right welds first

Build your TIG skills step by step, in this order:

  1. Start with straight beads on plate.
  2. Move on to pad welds.
  3. Finish with T-joint fillet welds, which are great for developing control.

5. Don’t weld from a distance

Keep a close working position. For the best visibility and control, your face shield should be 150-200mm from the arc.

6. Double the gas on open stainless corners

When DC TIG welding open outside corner joints on stainless steel, double your gas flow. This ensures proper shielding and helps prevent oxidation.

7. What amperage do I need to TIG weld steel?

Rule of thumb: 25 Amps per 1mm of material thickness.

Example: welding 3mm steel plate = 3 x 25, so set the current to around 75 Amps.

8. What amperage do I need to TIG weld aluminium?

Aluminium needs more heat than steel.

Rule of thumb: 35 Amps per 1mm of material thickness.

Example: 3mm aluminium = 3 x 35 = approx. 105 Amps.

9. Watch the weld colour

Colour is a key quality indicator, so check it after every run.

  • Clean weld: shiny silver or gold.
  • Bad weld: black or grey, which likely means poor gas shielding.

TIG rules of thumb: quick reference

SettingRule of thumbExample

Tungsten stick-out (gas lens)Equal to nozzle ID25mm nozzle = approx. 25mm stick-out
Post-flow5 seconds per 1mm of tungsten diameter2.4mm tungsten = 12 seconds
Working distanceFace shield 150-200mm from the arc
Open outside corners, stainless (DC TIG)Double the gas flow
Amperage, steel25 Amps per 1mm of thickness3mm steel = approx. 75 Amps
Amperage, aluminium35 Amps per 1mm of thickness3mm aluminium = approx. 105 Amps

Put the rules to work

Several of these tips depend on your torch setup. Rule 2 assumes a gas lens, so if you haven’t got one, look at our TIG gas lens collet bodies and matching gas lens cups. For rule 3 you need to know your tungsten diameter, and our RE4 rare-earth tungstens suit both AC and DC work. Not sure your torch suits your machine? Start with our TIG torch selection guide.

title: Welding fume extractor suction: what really affects it
content:
Welding fume extractor suction power varies a lot more between brands than the spec sheets suggest. Two units can look almost identical from the outside and perform very differently once the filter starts loading up. Here is what actually drives suction power, why the maximum airflow figure only tells part of the story, and what to check before you buy your next welding fume extractor.

That applies whether you are looking at a mobile extractor, a downdraft table or a torch extractor. Each one is a box with a fan and a filter, yet the design differences inside have a big impact on how well it does its job.

Why does suction power matter so much?

You buy an extractor to remove fume from the workplace, so the shop is safer, compliant and more pleasant to work in. Whether you spent your own money or talked your employer into funding it, the last thing you want is to find out it does not remove fume effectively. Sadly, that can and does happen. With so many brands and models on the market, they are not all built to the same standard.

Think of a vacuum cleaner with weak suction. It might have seemed like a bargain at first, but when it struggles to do the job it quickly becomes a frustrating waste of money. Compare that to a high-powered vacuum that makes cleaning effortless. No contest.

Fume extractors are the same. If you or your team are constantly battling an underperforming unit, you will eventually need or want to replace it, and that wastes both time and money.

How useful is the airflow rating?

The airflow rating, usually shown in cubic metres per hour (m³/hr), is one indication of how well a fume extractor will perform. Most manufacturers quote a maximum airflow rating, which lets you compare makes and models. Keep two limits in mind:

  • Maximum airflow is measured with a new, unused filter. It gives no indication of how the unit performs under load, once the filter starts to fill with fume dust.
  • The rating is often a very imprecise measurement, taken under very favourable conditions that don’t reflect real-life use, such as with the suction arm removed or completely straight.

What influences fume extractor suction performance?

Building an extractor with both effective filtration and good suction power is harder than it looks. Improving one often hurts the other, so getting the best overall design takes careful application of science (aerodynamics and aeroacoustics) plus experience. These are the main factors.

1. Internal and external design

From the outside, different makes and models can look more or less identical. Inside, there are often subtle design differences that significantly affect aerodynamic efficiency and suction power.

  • Aerodynamics: differences in internal design, especially upstream of the fan (from the extraction point, through the filter, to the fan), affect air volume and how smooth or turbulent the airflow is.
  • Leakage: no fume extractor is 100% airtight. There is always some leakage, where air is drawn in from points other than the intended suction point. The higher the leakage, the less efficient the unit and the less suction power it has.
  • Size: most operators prefer a smaller unit with a smaller footprint. Reducing the size of an extractor can restrict airflow volume, though. Smaller is not always better.
  • Fan and motor: the size and shape of the fan impeller, and the type of motor used, also affect suction power.

2. Filter design and size

Standard vs HEPA filters. Many extractors are offered with high-efficiency filters such as HEPA (e.g. H13 grade), which filter out smaller particles than standard filters such as F9 grade. That sounds like an obvious advantage. Be aware that a higher grade filter reduces airflow and suction power. It also collects more fume dust, which cuts airflow further as the filter fills.

As a result, a HEPA filter may not improve overall air quality in every application. The filtered air will be cleaner than with a standard filter, but the volume of filtered air may be lower, which can mean a higher fume concentration in the work environment.

Filter size. A filter with a larger surface area allows higher airflow and volume. Always weigh this up alongside the type of filter system, because some filters with a larger surface area clog faster and lose suction. We cover filter types in more detail in do mobile welding fume extractors work?

3. Manufacturer expertise and experience

An experienced manufacturer of welding fume extractors brings clear advantages in performance, reliability and long-term value. Over time they refine their designs using real-world feedback, which makes their systems more effective at capturing and filtering hazardous fume. Their products are typically built to higher quality standards, so they perform consistently and hold up in demanding industrial environments.

Established manufacturers also tend to offer better support, spare parts availability and compliance with safety regulations. That gives you more peace of mind and less risk of costly downtime or replacement.

The ALLCLEAR advantage

ALLCLEAR® by Weldclass is a market-leading brand that has delivered welding-specific fume control to Aussie welders and metal fabricators for over 15 years. With ALLCLEAR you get what you pay for: powerful fume extraction, reliability and features that make a difference on the job.

Start with our guide to choosing the right welding fume extractor, and once you have one, keep it pulling hard with the maintenance schedule for mobile welding fume extractors.

See it working before you buy

Spec sheets only go so far. The best test of suction is seeing a unit capture fume on a job like yours. Request a quote or a demo of the ALLCLEAR range, or find your nearest Weldclass distributor.

faq.a: A PAPR welding helmet combines a welding helmet with a powered air purifying respirator, giving the wearer filtered, powered air while they weld. The powered air adds comfort, and the helmet allows unrestricted movement. Keep in mind it only protects the person wearing it, depends on battery power and needs regular filter replacement.

faq.q: What standard should a PAPR welding helmet meet in Australia?
faq.a: Respiratory protection used in Australia should comply with AS/NZS 1716, the standard for respiratory protective devices. When buying PAPR welding helmets for a school, TAFE or university program, confirm compliance with AS/NZS 1716 alongside the helmet's optical clarity and protection ratings. title: Oxy acetylene equipment maintenance and safe use guide
content:
Oxy acetylene equipment maintenance follows a set rhythm under AS 4839-2001: a weekly visual check and leak test on everything, six-monthly or yearly function tests, and refurbishment of regulators, flashback arrestors and blowpipes at no more than five years. This guide sets out that schedule, then walks through safe setup, leak testing, lighting up and shutting down.

It is written for Weldclass gas and oxy-fuel equipment, but most of the steps are general best practice that applies to other brands too.

Maintenance schedule for gas and oxy-fuel equipment

This schedule aligns with the requirements of AS 4839-2001 The Safe Use of Portable and Mobile Oxy-fuel Gas Systems for Welding, Cutting, Heating and Allied Processes.

EquipmentWeeklyAs nominatedRefurbishment
Gas regulatorsVisual examination to determine suitability for service, checking for any signs of damage, the condition of threads and sealing surfaces, and any evidence of oil or grease contamination. Leak test all joints and connections at working pressure.Six monthly: functional tests to ensure correct operation of internal components.Manufacturer or supplier recommendation, but not exceeding five years.*
Flashback arrestorsVisual examination to determine suitability for service (e.g. gas, pressure rating, damage), condition of threads and sealing surfaces, and oil or grease contamination. Leak test all joints at working pressure.Yearly as detailed in AS 4603, or following a flashback: proper functioning of non-return valves.Not exceeding five years.
Hose assembliesVisual examination to determine suitability for service (e.g. gas, pressure rating, damage), condition of the cover, and threads and sealing surfaces of the end fittings. Leak test all joints at working pressure.Six monthly: check for absence of cuts and excessive wear by bending the hose in a tight radius, to ensure reinforcement is not visible.Determined by the hose assembly condition.
Blowpipes, mixers and attachmentsVisual examination for damage to the threads and sealing surfaces of the hose connections and the attachment connections. Leak test all joints at working pressure.Six monthly: test control valve function. Blank the attachment connection and leak test for internal malfunction.Manufacturer or supplier recommendation, but not exceeding five years.*

*Regulator elastomers and seals wear and deteriorate in service, and also deteriorate out of service. Items stored for one year or more without use should receive inspection as per the annual maintenance inspection.

What are the key safety rules for oxy-fuel gear?

  • Keep oil and grease away. Grease, oil and substances containing carbon (e.g. sawdust) can cause an explosion when in contact with oxygen. Never let gas equipment contact them, and keep all equipment clean at all times.
  • Wear protective gear and keep hair and loose clothing away from flames.
  • Check for leaks at all joints before each use with leak detection fluid or soapy water. Never use fire.
  • Use flashback arrestors at both ends of the hose. If a flashback occurs, shut off the valves immediately and inspect for damage.
  • Only trained professionals should repair or modify the equipment.

What hose should you use?

Use certified hoses and flashback arrestors. Twin hoses should be 5-10mm in diameter. When assembling hoses:

  • Choose the correct type and diameter.
  • Use approved fittings and clamps.
  • Make sure connections are tight and leak-free.
  • Avoid twisting or overheating hoses.
  • Replace worn or damaged hoses.

Our gas hose range includes ready-made oxy/acetylene hose sets and oxy/LPG sets.

How do you set up an oxy-fuel system?

The equipment is compatible with oxygen and acetylene cylinders, or oxygen and LPG cylinders. Before assembly:

  • Confirm all parts are in good condition.
  • Install flashback arrestors at both ends.
  • Tighten all connections.
  • Keep hoses clear of heat and damage.
  • Inspect the torch and fittings.

Assembly steps

  1. Connect the hoses to the torch and regulators.
  2. Attach the flashback arrestors.
  3. Connect the regulators to the cylinders.
  4. Secure the hoses to the arrestors.
  5. Check all fittings.
  6. Close the torch valves.
  7. Open the cylinder valves slowly.
  8. Set the regulator pressure.
  9. Test for leaks with leak detection fluid or soapy water.

How do you leak test oxy-acetylene equipment?

  1. Close all valves.
  2. Open the cylinder valves and set the pressure.
  3. Apply leak detection fluid to the joints. Never use a flame to test.
  4. If you find a leak, shut the valves, release the pressure, tighten the joints and re-test.
  5. If leaks persist, stop using the equipment and contact your supplier.

How do you light and shut down an oxy torch?

Ignition procedure

  1. Confirm the setup is secure and leak-free.
  2. Slightly open the fuel valve.
  3. Ignite with a spark lighter, such as a flint lighter. Never use matches.
  4. Slowly open the oxygen valve and adjust the flame.
  5. If the flame is unstable, shut down and inspect.

Never aim the torch at people.

Shutdown procedure

  1. Close the fuel valve.
  2. Close the oxygen valve.
  3. Shut the cylinder valves.
  4. Release pressure via the torch valves.
  5. Close the torch valves.
  6. Store the equipment safely.

Key reminders

  • Use the correct flashback arrestors.
  • Always test for leaks, and never use a flame to do it.
  • Wear safety gear.
  • Keep hoses away from heat.
  • Never point the torch at people.
  • Don’t use damaged equipment.

Book in the checks and stick to them

The weekly check takes a few minutes and is your best chance to catch a leak or a contaminated fitting early. Put the six-monthly and yearly tests in the diary and keep a record. If you are replacing worn gear, a complete PLATINUM oxy/acetylene kit is often simpler than patching an old set. Find a Weldclass distributor for parts, regulators and hose.

Be outstanding.

The information given is of a general nature only and does not take into account the specific circumstances of any individual application or situation, and should not be used as a substitute for professional advice. All applicable safety standards (including Australian standards), industry guidelines and regulations should be consulted and followed. E.&O.E.

faq.a: Under the AS 4839-2001 aligned schedule, give regulators a weekly visual check and leak test at working pressure, plus six-monthly functional tests of the internal components. faq.a: Check them visually and leak test the joints weekly. Test that the non-return valves work properly every year, as detailed in AS 4603, and also after any flashback. Flashback arrestors should be refurbished or replaced at no more than five years, and fitted at both ends of the hose.

faq.a: Grease, oil and substances containing carbon, such as sawdust, can cause an explosion when they come into contact with oxygen.
