title: Welding blanket materials: what are they made of?
content:
Welding blanket materials range from cowhide leather (typically 200°C max) through fibreglass (up to 500°C) to silica glass (up to 1100°C) and carbon fibre felt (up to 1000°C and more). No single material does it all. Each fabric has its own temperature resistance, price point and trade-offs, so the right welding blanket depends on the job. This guide compares each material so you can match a blanket or drape to your application.

What is the best welding blanket material?

It depends on the application. Start with the heat you need to handle, then weigh up spark resistance, comfort, chemical exposure and cost. Use the material comparison below together with our welding blanket selection chart to match the best Weldclass blanket to your work.

Welding blanket materials compared

This table sets out the materials welding blankets are typically made from, with their advantages and disadvantages.

MaterialSome advantagesSome disadvantages / further commentsWeldclass blanket examples
Cowhide leather
  • High density, resists spark penetration
  • Non-irritant
  • Economical
  • Relatively strong
  • Relatively low temperature resistance (typically 200°C max)
  • Can absorb oils and solvents, which can then become a fire hazard
 PROMAX Leather
Glass fibre (fibreglass)
  • Typical temperature resistance of up to 500°C; may handle higher temperatures if specially treated or coated
  • Strong and chemical resistant
  • Economical
  • Can shed fibres and dust, which is irritating and uncomfortable to handle
  • Being a woven fabric, sparks can penetrate the blanket after some wear and tear
  • Coatings can reduce irritation and improve durability, however some coatings have lower temperature resistance than the fabric, and can burn and give off undesirable or even toxic fumes
 PROMAX WB550
PROMAX WB1000
Silica glass
  • High temperature resistance of up to 1100°C
  • Softer and more flexible than fibreglass, more comfortable to handle
  • Very low thermal conductivity, which makes it particularly effective where you need to maintain consistent temperatures and prevent heat loss or gain
  • More comfortable than fibreglass but can still shed fibres and dust
  • Not as strong as fibreglass
  • Being a woven fabric, sparks can penetrate the blanket after some wear and tear
  • Coatings can reduce irritation and improve durability, however some coatings have lower temperature resistance than the fabric, and can burn and give off undesirable or even toxic fumes
 PROMAX WB1100
Carbon fibre / felt
  • High temperature resistance of up to 1000°C and more
  • Soft, flexible and non-irritant
  • Relatively lightweight
  • Very porous fabric that readily absorbs oils and solvents, which can then become a fire hazard
  • Less resistant to chemicals than fibreglass
  • Higher cost than fibreglass, especially in volume or larger sizes
  • Not recommended for heat treatment or stress relief
 Not currently offered by Weldclass
Bespoke materials
  • Attributes vary from product to product
  • One example is the Weldclass PLATINUM WB1250+ welding blanket, which offers new levels of safety and protection
 PLATINUM WB1250+

How do the main materials compare in practice?

Leather: dense and comfortable, for lower heat

Leather’s density stops sparks getting through, and it is easy on the skin. Its limit is heat, typically 200°C max. Keep leather blankets away from oils and solvents, because whatever they soak up can become a fire hazard.

Fibreglass: the economical all-rounder

Glass fibre is strong, chemical resistant and economical, with typical temperature resistance up to 500°C. The trade-off is handling. Fibres and dust can irritate, and as a woven fabric it can let sparks through once it is worn.

Silica glass: high heat and low thermal conductivity

Silica handles up to 1100°C and is softer and more flexible than fibreglass. Its very low thermal conductivity makes it a strong choice where you need to hold a consistent temperature. It isn’t as strong as fibreglass and can still shed some fibres.

Watch the coatings

Coatings on fibreglass and silica blankets can reduce irritation and improve durability. Check what the coating is rated to. Some have lower temperature resistance than the base fabric, and can burn and give off undesirable or even toxic fumes.

Bespoke materials

Some blankets use purpose-made materials whose attributes vary from product to product. Our PLATINUM WB1250+ welding blanket is one example, offering new levels of safety and protection.

Choose your welding blanket

Work out the maximum temperature your job throws at the blanket, then pick the material that handles it with the least compromise. Compare models in the selection chart linked above, then find a Weldclass distributor near you to see the range.

title: Gasless MIG wire: is it any good? Pros, cons and uses
content:
Yes, gasless MIG wire is good, provided you use it for the right jobs. Self-shielded flux-cored wire shines outdoors, on thicker material, on rusty or galvanised steel and anywhere a gas bottle is a nuisance. It falls short on sheet metal and on work where a clean, spatter-free finish matters most. Many welders swear by it, others say it isn’t as clean or strong as gas-shielded MIG. Here is how it really stacks up.

What is gasless MIG wire?

Gasless MIG wire, also called self-shielded flux-cored wire, is a welding wire that needs no external shielding gas. Its flux core creates its own protective gas when heated.

That makes it ideal outdoors, where wind can blow away the shielding gas used in conventional MIG welding. It also suits general work where getting rid of the gas cylinder improves portability and cuts cost.

Strictly speaking, gasless welding is a form of FCAW (flux cored arc welding), and calling it ‘MIG’ (metal inert gas) isn’t technically accurate. Because ‘MIG’ is so widely used to describe any welding from a spool of wire, we’ve taken the liberty of using it here.

What are the advantages of gasless MIG wire?

Great for outdoor use

This is the big one. Gas-shielded MIG needs a stable gas shield, which wind easily disturbs. Flux-cored wire generates its own protection, so it is more reliable in less-than-ideal conditions.

Better penetration

Flux-cored wire generally penetrates deeper than solid MIG wire. At the same output (amps), gasless wire will often weld thicker material than standard gas MIG wire. That is why it is popular on smaller machines with limited output, and for medium to heavy material.

Portability and convenience

No gas bottle means a lighter, more portable setup. It is ideal for fieldwork, farm repairs and job sites where mobility matters.

Works on rusty or dirty metal

Gasless wire is more forgiving on dirty, rusty or painted metal. The flux helps clean the weld pool, so you need less surface preparation.

Great for galvanised steel

Welding ‘gal’ is harder than uncoated or black steel and produces more spatter and fume. A good quality gasless wire can often outperform solid wire with gas here, because the flux helps remove and burn off the zinc coating. That reduces spatter and problems like porosity.

What are the disadvantages of gasless MIG wire?

More spatter and clean-up

Gasless welding produces more spatter and slag than gas-shielded MIG, so expect extra clean-up after welding.

Not as clean as gas-shielded MIG

Gas-shielded MIG typically gives cleaner welds with less porosity and a better appearance. If looks and minimal post-weld clean-up are the priority, gas-shielded MIG with a solid steel MIG wire may be the better option.

Limited on thin metal

Flux-cored wire is great on thick material but can be too hot for thin metal, which leads to burn-through. For sheet metal, a gas-shielded MIG setup is usually the better choice.

More fumes

Flux-cored welding produces more smoke and fume than conventional MIG welding. Proper ventilation or a welding fume extractor is essential to keep the workspace safe.

Gasless vs gas-shielded MIG at a glance

FactorGasless (self-shielded flux-cored)Gas-shielded MIG (solid wire)
Outdoors and windPerforms well, makes its own shieldingNeeds a stable gas shield
PenetrationGenerally deeper for the same ampsLess than flux-cored
Gas bottleNot requiredRequired
Rusty, dirty or painted metalMore forgivingNeeds more surface preparation
Galvanised steelGood quality wire often performs betterMore spatter and porosity issues
Thin sheet metalCan be too hot, risk of burn-throughUsually the better choice
Spatter, slag and clean-upMoreLess
Weld appearanceLess cleanCleaner, less porosity
FumeMore smoke and fumeLess

Is gasless MIG wire strong?

For most general applications, gasless wire is plenty strong enough. A reputable gasless wire such as our PLATINUM GL-11 gasless wire has typical tensile and yield strength higher than general-purpose stick welding rods.

For critical applications, especially construction and repair of heavy equipment where welds face very high loads or sudden, severe stress, general gasless wire may not be the best choice. Gas-covered flux-cored wire or specialist gasless wires may be needed instead.

For more detail, see Comparing strength of common welding wires and electrodes.

Is gasless MIG wire right for you?

Gasless MIG wire is an excellent option if:

  • you need to weld outdoors or in windy conditions
  • you’re working on thicker material (not sheet metal) or need more penetration
  • portability matters and carrying a gas bottle isn’t practical
  • you don’t mind extra spatter and weld appearance isn’t the top priority.

If you’re welding thinner material such as sheet metal, or you need very clean, good-looking welds, gas-shielded MIG may be the better choice.

Our view: gasless wire earns its place in any welder’s kit, especially for DIYers, farmers, construction workers and mobile welders. It has downsides, but its versatility and ease of use make it the right call in a lot of situations.

Find the right gasless wire

Browse the full Weldclass gasless wire range, including PLATINUM GL-11, which we call Australia’s #1 gasless wire, and handy gasless mini-spools for small machines. Then find a Weldclass distributor to pick some up.

faq.q: Do you need gas for gasless MIG wire?
faq.a: No. Gasless MIG wire is self-shielded flux-cored wire. The flux in the core creates its own protective gas when heated, so there is no external shielding gas and no cylinder to carry. That is why it is popular for outdoor work, farm repairs and mobile welding where portability matters.

faq.a: For most general applications, yes. A reputable gasless wire such as Weldclass PLATINUM GL-11 has typical tensile and yield strength higher than general-purpose stick welding rods. faq.a: Yes, and a good quality gasless wire often performs better than solid wire with gas on galvanised steel. faq.a: Usually not. Flux-cored wire penetrates deeply and can be too hot for thin metal, which leads to burn-through. For sheet metal, a gas-shielded MIG setup with solid wire is normally the better choice and also gives a cleaner finish with less clean-up.

faq.a: The flux core burns to create the shielding gas and slag, so flux-cored welding produces more smoke and fume than conventional gas-shielded MIG welding. Proper ventilation or a welding fume extractor is essential to keep your workspace safe, especially when welding indoors.

title: PAPR welding helmet maintenance: daily to annual schedule
content:
PAPR welding helmet maintenance is mostly about airflow. A clean filter, a charged battery and a sealed hose are what keep filtered air reaching your face, so they get checked every day. Below is our recommended daily, weekly and annual schedule, the pre-use check you should run before every shift, and the general care rules for cleaning and storage.

It is written for Weldclass respirator welding helmets, but most of the steps are general best practice that applies to most brands of PAPR welding helmets.

Which helmets and respirators does this cover?

This schedule applies to these Weldclass models:

  • PROMAX 680R welding helmet with PAPR respirator
  • PROMAX 850R welding helmet with PAPR respirator
  • PROMAX R50 PAPR respirator unit

PAPR welding helmet maintenance schedule

The schedule below covers the respirator (blower) unit, the hose and the welding helmet.

FrequencyAction / componentDetails
DailyVisual inspectionCheck for any visible damage or wear. Ensure all components are free from obstruction and debris.
DailyFilter checkInspect the condition of the main filter, pre-filter and spark filter mesh. Replace if visibly clogged or damaged. Note: the main filter should be replaced no later than 40 hours of use or 30 days, whichever comes first, and immediately if visibly clogged or if airflow is restricted.
DailyFunction checkComplete the pre-use checks as per the pre-use check procedure below (or section 11b of the user manual).
DailyCover lensesEnsure all clear cover lenses are clean. Replace if scratched or damaged. Note: for correct and safe operation of the helmet, the front cover lens must not have any blemish or marks that obstruct the view of the arc sensors on the front of the auto-darkening lens.
DailyBatteryRemove the respirator battery and inspect its condition. If there are any signs of damage, dispose of and replace the battery. Ensure the battery is fully charged before the work shift.
WeeklyClean exteriorWipe with a damp cloth to remove dust and debris.
WeeklyClean internalsCheck the helmet headgear, air vent and internal surfaces, and clean if required.
WeeklyInspect hoseIf the inside of the hose is dirty, or there are leaks or creases, replace the hose.
WeeklyInspect / clean face sealClean the face seal with a damp cloth and mild detergent, or machine wash in cold water on a gentle/delicate cycle. Replace the face seal if excessively dirty, damaged, torn or punctured.
WeeklyInspect for damageCheck all components for damage, cracks, wear, air leaks and so on. Replace parts as required.
AnnualReplace partsReplace all filters, the helmet face seal, hose and hose cover, helmet cover lenses and helmet sweatband. Replacing the respirator battery is recommended if you estimate the existing battery has exceeded 500 charge cycles.
AnnualUpdate recordsEnsure maintenance tasks are logged. Review records to ensure compliance with this schedule.

How do you do a PAPR pre-use check?

Run this check every day before using the welding helmet with respirator. Do it in a safe environment that is free of fumes and other hazards.

  1. Ensure the battery is fully charged.
  2. Disconnect the air hose from the blower unit.
  3. Insert the flowmeter device into the blower unit and switch it on.
  4. Check whether the ball indicator reaches the minimum flow level marking. If yes, the unit is suitable for use. If no, replace the filters and test again*.
  5. Attach the air hose to the blower unit and switch it on.
  6. Block the end (outlet) of the hose by hand until the alarm sounds and the blower vibrates*.
  7. Check that all components, including the helmet, face seal, hose, blower unit, filters and battery, are in good condition and assembled correctly.

*If minimum flow is not reached and/or the blower unit alarms do not work, the unit may have a malfunction and/or need replacing. Re-test with a new, fully charged battery and new filters. If the malfunction continues, contact your Weldclass distributor and/or replace the blower with a new unit.

General care and maintenance guidelines

Cleaning

Clean with mild detergent and a damp cloth. Do not use solvents or alcohol-based cleaning agents. Do not immerse the unit in water or spray it directly with liquids.

Storage and disposal

  • Store in a dry, clean area with an ambient temperature range of -10 to 55°C and relative humidity below 90% RH.
  • If stored below 0°C, let the battery warm up before charging or use so it reaches full capacity.
  • If the respirator will not be used for a long time, remove the battery, fully charge it and store it separately.
  • At the end of the working life of the unit and/or battery, follow local, state and national regulations for disposal.

Where can you buy PAPR spare parts?

Replacement parts for the R50 blower unit are listed under PROMAX R50 respirator spare parts. Replacement face seals are in shell parts for welding helmets, and you will find outer and inner cover lenses in our welding helmet lens range. Sweatbands for the annual change-out are also in our helmet spares range.

If you are still choosing a respirator helmet for a training workshop, read our guide to choosing a PAPR welding helmet for education and training.

Make the check part of the shift

The pre-use check takes a couple of minutes and tells you straight away whether the blower is delivering. Keep spare filters and a charged battery on hand so a failed check does not stop work. For parts or advice, find a Weldclass distributor near you.

title: Mobile welding fume extractors: do they work?
content:
A mobile welding fume extractor (often called a fume cart) works well in many Australian workshops. It captures fume at the source and rolls to wherever the welding is happening. It is not the best answer for every job, though. Below we compare mobile units with fume extraction torches, PAPR welding helmets and ducted central systems, then cover the design differences between extractors that decide how well they perform and what they cost to run.

What is a mobile welding fume extractor?

A mobile welding fume extractor is a portable unit that removes harmful fumes and particulate matter generated during welding. It typically has a flexible arm or hose that you position near the welding area to capture fume at the source.

The unit filters the captured air to remove contaminants, giving a safer and cleaner working environment. Wheels or casters let you move it to different areas of the workshop as needed.

How do mobile fume extractors compare with other fume control systems?

There are four main types of welding fume extraction system: mobile fume extractors, fume extraction MIG and TIG torches, PAPR welding helmets and ducted central systems. Here are the key pros and cons of each.

Fume control systemProsCons
Mobile fume extractor
  • Extracts fumes at the source
  • Can be moved to different locations
  • Versatile: easily deployed, and used only where and when each operator needs it
  • Easy to maintain
  • Does not interfere with operator ergonomics or comfort
  • Depending on model and brand, suits a wide range of applications including MIG, Stick, TIG, grinding, plasma, oxy and gouging
  • Needs to be moved manually to the fume source or welding location
  • In very confined spaces, wall-mounted or other systems may be a better option
  • May not be ideal where the welder has to move very frequently over a wide area
Fume extraction MIG or TIG welding torch
  • Extracts fumes directly at the point of generation for high-efficiency removal
  • No extra set-up or movement needed, as the extraction point is always at the fume source
  • Not suitable for grinding, Stick/MMA welding, plasma cutting or gouging
  • Typically not suitable for vertical or overhead welding, or where space at the weld joint is confined
  • High set-up cost: fume torches cost substantially more than standard torches, and each torch needs a dedicated extraction unit
  • Torch is bulkier, heavier and more cumbersome than a standard torch (some are better than others)
  • Ongoing cost of torch consumables can be significantly higher than standard torches
Welding helmet with PAPR respirator
  • Relatively low initial purchase cost
  • Very mobile and allows unrestricted movement
  • Quick and easy to deploy
  • Powered air gives the operator extra comfort
  • Only protects the user
  • Does not remove fumes from the environment, or protect others in it
  • Depends on battery power
  • Requires frequent filter replacement, with the associated operating cost
  • Operator carries extra weight and bulk
Ducted or central fume extraction system
  • Extracts fumes at the source
  • Suits large-scale workshops, especially where all workstations are typically active at the same time
  • Minimal maintenance or downtime for operators
  • High cost
  • Time-consuming to procure and install
  • Can be inefficient if workstations are used at different times, or some are not always in use
  • Not suitable where portability and flexibility are required

For most workshops where operators work at different stations, on different processes, at different times, a mobile extractor is the practical middle ground. A PAPR helmet such as the PROMAX 850R adds comfort and personal protection for the welder, but remember it only protects the person wearing it.

Are all mobile weld fume extractors the same?

They do the same job and can look similar, but there are fundamental differences under the hood between welding smoke extractor brands and models. Those differences affect:

  • Performance
  • Unit cost
  • Operating (or lifetime) cost

These are the main differences to check before you buy.

1. Airflow and suction capacity

You don’t want to invest in a fume extractor only to find it lacks the airflow or suction to do the job. Airflow rates (m³/hr) vary significantly between brands and models, so check them. Keep in mind that airflow is measured with a new, clean filter, so the advertised figure is not the whole story.

Airflow typically drops as the filter fills, because there is more obstruction to the air. The result is lower suction and reduced extraction efficiency. This is more significant with some filter systems than others, as the graph below shows.

2. Replacement filter costs

This is often not given enough thought before buying an extraction unit. Ask two questions: what do replacement filters cost, and how often will I need to replace them?

Replacement filters can cost anywhere from around $500 to well over $1,000. The price alone means little without some indication of service life. A filter that costs more than others can last longer in service and give a lower overall cost.

How long a filter will last is a “how long is a piece of string” question. Volume of fume, frequency of use and many other variables affect service life, so most manufacturers will only give a ballpark figure at best. To compare lifetime filter costs between one unit and another, you need to understand the type of filter system each one uses.

3. Filter system

All mobile extractors have replaceable filters. The main types are box filters, disposable filters, remove-to-clean filters, in-situ cleanable filters and auto-cleaning filters. They compare as follows.

Which filter type is best in a mobile fume extractor?

Cleanable filters win on running cost and on keeping suction steady. Box and disposable filters are convenient to swap, but you pay for that convenience every time one clogs.

Filter typeProsCons
Box (or cassette) filter
Usually box-shaped, typically a main filter plus a pre-filter.
  • Can be larger, with more surface area, so it lasts longer in a single-use comparison
  • Replacing rather than cleaning can be more convenient for the operator
  • Pre-filter stops larger particles entering the main filter and can be replaced at lower cost
  • No compressed air needed (for cleaning)
  • Not cleanable or re-usable
  • More frequent main filter replacement and cost
  • Pre-filter replacement costs and downtime
  • Operating cost over the service life of the extractor is typically much higher than with cleanable filters
  • With no way to clean it, airflow (suction) decreases as the filter fills and the unit and motor have to work harder
  • The larger the filter, the more strain on the motor
  • Operators may replace filters before they are completely full to fix the airflow drop (more cost)
  • Every particle, large or small, that enters the unit settles on or in the filter, so it clogs faster and airflow drops
  • May not be practical for high fume applications (eg some flux-cored wires) due to very fast clogging
  • All particles, including any hot sparks, are drawn onto or into the filter, which increases the risk of burnout or fire
Disposable (non-cleanable) cartridge filter
Single disposable unit, without pre-filters.
  • Can be larger, with more surface area, so it lasts longer in a single-use comparison
  • Replacing rather than cleaning can be more convenient for the operator
  • No compressed air needed (for cleaning)
  • Not cleanable or re-usable
  • More frequent filter replacement and cost
  • Filters can cost more due to their size
  • Operating cost over the service life of the extractor is typically much higher than with cleanable filters
  • With no way to clean it, airflow (suction) decreases as the filter fills and the unit and motor have to work harder
  • The larger the filter, the more strain on the motor
  • Operators may replace filters before they are completely full to fix the airflow drop (more cost)
Remove-to-clean filter
Designed to be cleaned with a compressed air nozzle and re-used. The filter must be removed from the unit to be cleaned.
  • Lower operating costs, as filters are designed to be cleaned and re-used
  • With cleaning, airflow (suction) is higher and more consistent
  • Filter has to be removed for cleaning, which exposes the operator to collected fume dust
  • Prolonged cleaning downtime to remove and refit the filter
  • Units are typically low cost, with comparatively poor airflow and suction
ALLCLEAR in-situ cleanable filter
Designed to be cleaned with a compressed air nozzle through a special access door, then re-used.
  • Significantly lower operating costs, as filters are designed to be cleaned and re-used many times
  • In-situ cleaning (no need to remove the filter)
  • Special cleaning access door, so the operator is not exposed to captured fume dust
  • No pre-filter to replace, which reduces cost further
  • With cleaning, airflow (suction) is higher and more consistent, and the motor does not have to work against a large volume of dust in the filter
  • Some operator downtime to clean filters periodically (unless the unit has auto cleaning, see below)
  • Requires access to compressed air for cleaning
ALLCLEAR auto-cleanable filter
Designed to be cleaned with compressed air by a built-in automatic cleaning system, then re-used.
  • Same advantages as the in-situ filter above, plus:
  • Saves operator downtime (start the cleaning cycle at the end of a shift and walk away)
  • Extends filter life and reduces costs even further, thanks to very even, automated pulse jet cleaning that keeps the filter in good condition
  • Allows many more (hundreds of) use cycles per filter before replacement is required
  • Frequent, very thorough cleaning further improves airflow consistency and reduces flow drop
  • Allows use in high fume applications (eg flux-cored wires)
  • Requires access to compressed air for cleaning
ALLCLEAR spark deflector
As well as cleanable filters, ALLCLEAR units have a spark deflection plate that shields the main filter from coarse particles and sparks and redirects them to a dust collection tray or bin.
  • Further increases filter life and reduces costs by keeping larger particles out of the filter
  • Significantly reduces the risk of fire, as sparks and larger hot particles are diverted away from the filter
  • A fixed component, so it does not rely on an operator remembering to replace a spark filter
n/a

ALLCLEAR mobile welding smoke extractors by Weldclass

The ALLCLEAR range of mobile fume extractors has been tried and proven in Australia for many years. ALLCLEAR units combine features that keep delivering value long after the purchase:

  • Low operating costs and proven reliability
  • 7 Year Warranty offer
  • Cleanable cartridge filter for extended life and significantly lower filter replacement costs
  • Exceptional suction power, with a maximum airflow rate of up to 3,500 m³/hr
  • Cleanable cartridge allows consistent suction, with minimal flow drop
  • Spark deflection system shields filters from coarse particles and sparks and redirects them to the dust collection tray or bin, significantly reducing the risk of burnout and further increasing filter life
  • Large surface area filters with high filtration efficiency
  • Patented dust collection tray or bin allows fast, safe removal of dust ejected during filter cleaning
  • Exhaust airflow is directed upwards and away from the floor, for minimal disturbance of dust in the surrounding area
  • 100% Australian owned, operated and supported
  • Range of units available with manual or auto cleaning, 1ph or 3ph power, and single or twin arms

For high fume work or busy multi-shift workshops, an auto-cleaning model such as the ALLCLEAR MA350 AUTO is the one to look at, because it allows use with flux-cored wires and saves operator time on cleaning.

Contact our fume control team for a quote or demonstration, or find an ALLCLEAR distributor near you. Once your extractor is running, follow our mobile fume extractor maintenance schedule to keep the suction where it should be.

faq.q: Do mobile welding fume extractors work?
faq.a: Yes. A mobile fume extractor captures fume at the source through a flexible arm or hose, filters it and returns cleaner air to the workshop. faq.a: A fume torch captures fume right at the point of generation and never needs repositioning. faq.a: An auto-cleaning unit uses built-in pulse jet cleaning with compressed air, so you can start a cycle at the end of a shift and walk away. title: Welding helmet switching speed: why faster isn’t always safer
content:
Welding helmet switching speed is the time an auto-darkening lens takes to go dark once its sensors detect the arc. Brands love to advertise it, and a faster number looks safer on the box. On its own, though, that number tells you very little about how well a helmet protects your eyes. Below we explain what switching speed means, what the Australian standard requires, and what to check instead when you choose a safe, compliant welding helmet.

What is welding helmet switching speed?

Switching speed is the time it takes an auto-darkening welding helmet lens to switch from the light shade (typically around shade 3-4) to the dark shade (anywhere from shade 6 to 14, depending on the helmet model) after the sensors detect the welding arc.

Is a faster switching speed safer?

For many years, switching speeds have been quoted as a measure of how safe a helmet is. The implication is that a helmet with a faster advertised speed is likely to be safer than one with a slower advertised speed. That is not necessarily the case.

In many cases the claimed switching speed is a nominal figure. It might be based on factory testing under the most ideal conditions, and it helps the helmet compare favourably against the switching speed claims of other brands.

Switching speed is also only one aspect of the optical protection a helmet provides. You wouldn’t judge a car only by its maximum rpm. In the same way, you can’t judge a welding helmet by its switching speed alone.

How do I know if a helmet has a safe switching speed?

The question “is this helmet safe to use?” is best answered by another question: does it conform to a reputable standard such as AS/NZS 1338.1? If a helmet has been independently tested and conforms to AS/NZS 1338.1, its switching speed is within safe margins.

Once switching speed is within the requirements of AS/NZS 1338.1, it makes no difference to safety whether the helmet is 10x or 100x faster than the standard requires. The reason is simple: the human eye can only detect speeds up to a certain point.

The human eye will not notice any difference below around 0.2ms. Anything faster than 0.2ms feels the same to the operator. So a helmet with a speed of 0.1ms will be no safer, and will feel no different, than a helmet with a speed of 0.2ms.

What are the AS/NZS 1338.1 switching speed requirements?

AS/NZS 1338.1 switching speed requirements vary depending on which shade the lens is switching from and which shade it is switching to. For example, for a shade 9-13 helmet with a light shade of 3 or 4, the maximum allowable switching speed ranges from 2ms (milliseconds) through to 200ms. That is a very wide margin (refer to AS/NZS 1338.1 clause 2.4.1).

Switching speeds can also vary with ambient temperature.

Both points are more reasons why a single advertised switching speed number doesn’t tell you the full story.

Why does arc detection matter more than switching speed?

Arc detection is very often overlooked in the switching speed discussion, yet it has the biggest effect on what the welder actually experiences.

The most important factor in how a welder perceives switching speed is the ability of the helmet or lens to detect the welding arc in the first place. If a lens has poor arc detection, or can’t detect the arc at the right time, it won’t switch when it should. At that point switching speed becomes almost irrelevant.

Example: TIG arc starts

TIG welding shows the problem clearly. An initial spark starts the welding process and ignites the arc. This happens when the operator first touches the tungsten electrode on the job, or, on machines with HF (high frequency) start, when the operator presses the torch trigger to initiate the HF start.

Many lenses and helmets can’t detect this initial spark. They only detect the stable, much brighter welding arc that occurs some time later. In that case, even if the switching speed is very fast, the helmet can seem slow to the operator.

What should you look for in an auto-darkening welding helmet?

Based on the points above, put these ahead of the advertised switching speed:

  • Independent testing and conformance to AS/NZS 1338.1. This is the best answer to whether the helmet is safe to use.
  • Reliable arc detection, particularly if you do TIG or other low-amperage work where the arc start is hard to sense.
  • UV and IR protection in light mode, so your eyes are still protected if the lens ever fails to switch to dark.

Switching speeds of Weldclass welding helmets

All Weldclass helmet models have been independently tested to, and conform to and/or exceed, the requirements of the AS/NZS 1338.1 standard.

All models also offer UV and IR protection in light mode. That means even if the lens were to fail to switch to dark, the operator is protected from the harmful UV and IR rays that cause permanent damage.

We are constantly improving the technology and electronics that drive the arc sensors, for reliable switching even in challenging applications and conditions such as low-amperage TIG welding.

Browse the full Weldclass welding helmet range to compare models. If you also need respiratory protection, a PAPR helmet such as the PROMAX 850R with PAPR respirator combines an auto-darkening lens with powered air. Our guide to choosing a PAPR welding helmet for education and training covers that decision in more detail, and replacement auto-darkening lenses and cassettes are available for existing helmets.

Choose the standard over the sales pitch

When you compare helmets, check for AS/NZS 1338.1 conformance first, then ask how the sensors handle low-amperage TIG starts. The advertised switching speed comes a distant third. content:

It covers rods and wires for brazing and welding steel, cast iron, stainless-steel, copper, brass, bronze, nickel alloys and aluminium. Find the material you’re joining, check which rods are marked ✓, then use the comments and melting ranges to narrow it down.

Brazing rod and TIG filler rod selection chart

*Oxy “fusion welding” of steel, stainless and aluminium is possible (although MIG and/or TIG are typically the best and most convenient, successful methods). It requires oxy-acetylene (not oxy/LPG) and a suitable flux. Weldclass does not supply flux products.

Which brazing rod should I use?

Start with the base metals, then the fit-up. Close-fitting parts suit a free-flowing silver rod. Poor fit-up suits a rod that is good at gap-filling. Here’s how the range breaks down.

Bronze brazing rods

Manganese Bronze is the general purpose option for joining and repairing most ferrous and copper-based metals, including steel and cast iron. It can be used in place of Tobin Bronze for many applications. Do not use it on copper pipes carrying hot or salt water. Melting range is 870-900°C.

Nickel Bronze (Nickel Silver) gives high strength and good wear resistance, and adds nickel alloys to the list of materials it can join. It is also used for build-up of ferrous components, such as repairing gear teeth. Melting range is 920-940°C.

Silver brazing rods

45% Silver is the general purpose, high strength silver rod. It has high fluidity, rapid capillary flow and good corrosion resistance, which makes it the pick for parts with close fit-up in HVAC, refrigeration and marine work. It is also the only rod in this chart marked suitable for stainless-steel brazing. Melting range is 640-680°C.

15% Silver (“phos copper”) joins copper-to-copper without flux, and brass-to-brass with flux. It is excellent for gap-filling where close fit-up does not exist, so it suits copper pipe, plumbing fittings, hot water tanks and joints subject to thermal expansion and service vibration. Melting range is 645-800°C.

2% Silver (“phos copper”) is the economic option. It joins copper to copper (with or without flux) and copper to low-zinc brass (flux required). Typical uses are copper pipe, plumbing fittings and hot water tanks. Melting range is 645-820°C.

The full range of silver and bronze brazing alloys is in our brazing rods category.

TIG and oxy filler rods

Steel S6 is for general purpose TIG welding, or oxy/acetylene fusion welding, of mild steel. It is good for poor fit-up and where impurities such as rust and scale are present.

Stainless-Steel 316L is for TIG welding common 300 series stainless steels.

Aluminium 5356 is for TIG welding a wide range of aluminium alloys.

See all TIG and oxy rods in our filler rods category.

Can you fusion weld with oxy instead of TIG?

Yes, oxy fusion welding of steel, stainless and aluminium is possible, although MIG and/or TIG are typically the best and most convenient methods. If you do go down the oxy path, you need oxy-acetylene (not oxy/LPG) and a suitable flux. Weldclass does not supply flux products.

For oxy brazing and welding gear, a PLATINUM oxy/acetylene kit with the right oxy/acetylene brazing tips covers most workshop jobs. Our article on maintenance and use of gas and oxy equipment will help you keep that setup safe.

Get the right rod for the job

Match the rod to the base metals and fit-up using the chart, and you will avoid most brazing headaches before you light the torch. Weldclass brazing and filler rods are stocked by distributors around Australia, so find a Weldclass distributor near you or contact our team if you need help with an unusual job.

title: Welding with a pacemaker: what you need to know
content:
We are often asked whether it is safe for someone with a pacemaker implant to use a welding machine. Welding with a pacemaker is a complex question that crosses from the industrial into the medical, and it is one only your doctor or cardiologist, together with the manufacturer of your device, can answer for you. Below we point you to expert articles on the topic and summarise the precautions they describe.

Always speak to your doctor and/or cardiologist first and follow their advice. Check with your device manufacturer about your specific implant as well.

Is it safe to weld with a pacemaker?

Welding under any conditions if you have a pacemaker implant will involve health and safety risks. The precautions further down may help to reduce those risks. They will not eliminate them.

We are a welding equipment supplier, not a medical authority. This article is a guide to other more detailed and authoritative sources, so read them in full and get medical advice before making any decisions.

What do the experts say?

  • Can I go near someone who is welding after having a pacemaker implanted? Dr. Brian Olshansky on ABC News.
  • The risks of using a heart pacemaker and welding. Article by TWI (The Welding Institute), UK.
  • FAQs for implantable cardiac devices: welding and chainsaws. Article by Medtronic USA, a cardiac device manufacturer.

How can you reduce the risk if you must weld?

The following points summarise the articles above. It is not a complete summary. If, after speaking with your doctor or cardiologist, you must weld, these steps may help to reduce (but will not eliminate) the risks involved:

  1. Keep the amperage range under 130A.
  2. Avoid using any welding machine with a Pulse function or a High-Frequency (HF) function. Pulse is typically found on some higher-end and professional TIG and MIG machines, but can be found on some Stick (MMA) machines as well. HF is typically found on professional TIG machines and some plasma cutters.
  3. Keep your clothing (including gloves and shoes) and your work area dry at all times.
  4. Keep at least 600mm (2 ft) between your pacemaker and the welding arc.
  5. Keep the welding cables and the welding machine as far from you as possible. The recommended distance for the welding unit is around 1.5m (5 ft) from where you work.
  6. Where possible, twist the welding cables together, and make sure the pacemaker user is not standing in a current loop, with the torch on one side and the return cable on the other.

What should you check before buying or using a welder?

Step 2 above means machine features matter. Before you use or buy a welder, check whether it has a Pulse or HF function. Our welding machine selector and the full range of Weldclass welders list each machine’s functions, and our team can confirm the features of a specific model if you contact us.

We can tell you what a machine does. Whether you should weld at all, and under what conditions, is a decision for you, your doctor or cardiologist, and your device manufacturer.

This article is intended to provide a guide and reference to other more detailed and authoritative articles on this topic, and should not be taken as expert medical advice. Always consult your doctor and/or cardiologist first and follow their advice. E.&O.E.

Which stick welding rod should I use for mild steel?

For most mild and galvanised steel work, a general purpose rod is the right call. PLATINUM 12V is very popular due to its exceptional user appeal: a very smooth arc, easy re-striking and self-releasing slag. PROMAX GP has the same attributes and comes in 1kg re-usable packs. Both are tolerant to dirty materials and poor fit-up, run on most welding machines and can be used in all positions, including vertical down.

When do you need a low hydrogen electrode?

Step up to a low hydrogen rod where higher strength is required, for example highly restrained joints or components subject to higher load or sudden stress.

  • PLATINUM 16XT is twin-coated for excellent arc stability, and its 2kg vacuum-sealed packs keep electrodes moisture-free. Use it on machines with an OCV of DC 55V or AC 65V and above.
  • PROMAX 16LH comes in 1kg re-usable packs that keep electrodes in good condition. Use it on machines with an OCV of 45-55V and above.

Both can be used in all positions except vertical down.

Which electrode for stainless-steel?

PLATINUM 316L is for welding matching 316, 316L and common 300 series stainless steels, including 301, 302, 304, 304L and 3Cr12. It has good resistance to pitting, acids and general corrosion, suits most welding machines and runs in all positions including vertical down.

PLATINUM 309MoL is the rod for joining stainless to mild or low alloy steels. It also welds matching 309 and 309L stainless, CrNi and CrNiMo stainless and hard to weld steels, and is used for cladding and buffer layers. It needs a machine with an OCV of 70V and above, and is used in all positions except vertical down.

Browse the full range of stainless-steel electrodes.

What if you don’t know what the steel is?

PLATINUM 312 is the universal option. It gives high strength welds on almost any steel or stainless-steel, which makes it ideal for unknown steels, dissimilar steels such as steel to stainless, and die or tool steel. It is also used as a buffer layer before hardfacing. It suits most welding machines and runs in all positions, including vertical down.

Which electrode for cast iron?

PLATINUM NiFe is for high strength, hot or cold welding of cast iron (including grey / malleable, nodular and SG iron) and for joining cast iron to steel. The weld deposit is machineable. It suits most welding machines, but use it in the flat / horizontal position only. You’ll find it with our other special purpose electrodes.

Which hardfacing electrode should I choose?

Both hardfacing rods are used in the flat / horizontal position only. The choice comes down to the type of wear and how much the part flexes.

  • PROMAX 700 (53-56 HRC) is for general use on ground-engaging implements and similar, such as augers, points, tynes and blades. It is ideal for parts subject to flexing and suits most welding machines.
  • PLATINUM 943 (60-65 HRC) is the high performance option for long wear life, with exceptional abrasion resistance and good impact strength. Use it on bucket lips, screws, hammers, teeth, crushers and the like, on machines with an OCV of 55V and above.

See all hardfacing electrodes.

Why does OCV matter when choosing an electrode?

Several rods in the chart list a minimum open circuit voltage (OCV): PLATINUM 16XT, PROMAX 16LH, PLATINUM 309MoL and PLATINUM 943. OCV is the voltage your welder puts out across its terminals before the arc is struck. Check your machine’s specifications before you buy these electrodes, and if you’re choosing a new machine, compare OCV across our stick and TIG welders.

Find the right rod near you

Pick the rod type from the chart, check the positions and your machine’s OCV, and you’re set. Weldclass electrodes are stocked by distributors across Australia, so find a Weldclass distributor near you or contact our team if you need help with a specific job.

Our line fill rate is the percentage of order lines we ship in full on a distributor’s order, first time. We call our monthly report the Supply-O-Meter. Why do back orders matter?

For years, a major frustration in the Australian welding industry has been unpredictable supply: poor product availability, high back-order rates and unreliable delivery time frames. If you’re a distributor, you know what back orders and delays do. They:

  • cost you business and upset your customers
  • cause friction and inefficiency
  • reduce your sales and kill opportunity
  • waste valuable time that could go into higher-value work.

We’re determined to be Australia’s most reliable welding supply partner. Publishing our line-fill rate every month keeps us honest.

What does line fill rate mean?

The rate shows the percentage of items or lines we supply on our distributors’ orders in the first instance. A rate of 98%, for example, means that out of every 100 items or lines, 98 are shipped in full and 2 have back orders.

title: TIG torch selection guide: choose the right torch for your welder
content:
This TIG torch selection guide gets you to the right torch for your welding machine fast, without the confusing mumbo-jumbo. It comes down to one question: does your machine have a TIG gas outlet fitting on the front? Answer that, check how your machine starts the arc, and the quick reference chart below points you to one of three torch types.

Which TIG torch suits my welder?

Use this quick reference chart to identify the type of TIG torch that suits your machine. Each torch type is explained in more detail below.

Welding machine typeTypical features / functionsTIG gas outlet fitting on front of machine?Suitable TIG torch
StandardBasic lift-arc (or scratch-start) TIG arc ignition. Usually DC-only, for TIG welding steel and stainless. Includes, but not limited to, many portable Stick/TIG or MIG/Stick/TIG welders.No. The gas hose on the torch connects directly to the gas regulator.Standard TIG torch with valve
Professional / specialisedHF TIG arc ignition. Usually AC/DC, for TIG welding all metals including aluminium. May have options such as a foot pedal and/or a water cooler for the torch.Yes. The gas hose on the torch connects to the front of the machine.Specialised TIG torch with switch and remote controls on the handle, or TK Super-Flex series

Standard TIG torches with valve

This is the torch for most portable inverter welders with a basic lift-arc or scratch-start TIG function.

  • Suits most inverter welders that have a basic lift-arc or scratch-start TIG function, including many portable DC inverter Stick/TIG or MIG/Stick/TIG machines.
  • For use on welding machines which do NOT have an internal TIG gas line or fitting.
  • The gas hose on the TIG torch connects directly to the gas regulator on the gas cylinder, and gas flow is controlled via the valve on the TIG torch head.
  • Weldclass standard TIG torches can be fitted to most brands and models of these machines.
  • Available in #17 (150 Amp) and #26 (200 Amp) series.

View Weldclass standard TIG torches with valve.

Specialised TIG torches with switch and remote controls on the torch handle

  • Used on machines which have a TIG gas outlet fitting on the front of the machine.
  • The torch has a switch (and may also have current / amps adjustment) on the handle, and a control cable with a plug that connects to a socket on the front of the machine.
  • Most AC/DC TIG welders use these torches, as do some DC Stick/TIG and MIG/Stick/TIG inverter welders, especially those with an HF start function.
  • While the torch head and similar parts may be common types, the control plug (the type of plug and its wiring configuration) is usually bespoke and brand / model specific. There are many different types of multi-pin plugs in use, and the wiring configuration can change from one machine to another depending on how the machine is programmed.

For that reason, we recommend you buy this type of torch from the manufacturer of your machine. If you need one for a Weldclass machine, see our specialised TIG torches to suit specific Weldclass machines.

PLATINUM TK Super-Flex TIG torches

  • Used where a lightweight, flexible and slimline torch is wanted for maximum dexterity, control and operator comfort.
  • For use on professional TIG welding machines (typically AC/DC machines).
  • Weldclass TK Super-Flex series TIG torches can be fitted to most brands and models of these machines.
  • Often used together with a foot pedal or controller, where a switch on the torch head is NOT required, as all controls and adjustments are made via the foot pedal.
  • Can also be optioned with a snap-on switch, if you want controls on the torch.

View Weldclass TK Super-Flex TIG torches, and if you’re setting up for pedal control, see our foot controllers for AC/DC TIG welders.

Get the torch sorted, then get welding

Check the front of your machine for a TIG gas outlet, match it to the chart and you’ll have the right torch first time. If you’re still choosing a machine, browse our Stick and TIG welders and multi-function machines, and once you’re set up, our 9 rules of thumb for TIG welding will help you dial it in. Weldclass torches are sold through distributors around Australia, so find a Weldclass distributor near you.

content:
Weldclass offers an industry-first 7 year warranty on machines, accessories and equipment. The 7 year warranty formalises this heritage of quality and care. It’s our way of extending the Weldclass experience to welders everywhere, and rewarding customers for trusting us with their investment.

Australian since 1979

In the early 1900s, the forebears of the founder of Weldclass pioneered mechanical engineering in Australia, then later invented metal coating technologies that are still used globally.

Today Weldclass remains a 100% Australian, family-owned company. We started in regional Australia, in Tamworth NSW, in 1979, and our head office is still there today.
